contentRule: Original concise study guidance derived from the assigned chapter scope; no textbook pages or source prose are published.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Units, vectors, and estimation
recognition: Start here when the obstacle is representation: converting units, resolving components, projecting one vector onto another, or checking whether an answer can be right before calculating.
keyIdeas: Dimensions constrain equations but do not determine dimensionless constants.
Choose a basis before writing components; a vector equation is basis-independent.
Dot products select parallel content; cross products encode perpendicular magnitude and orientation.
Order-of-magnitude estimates should expose dominant scales and ignored effects.
workflow: List base dimensions and convert every input to one unit system.
Draw axes and resolve vectors once.
Estimate the scale before exact arithmetic.
Check dimensions, sign, direction, and plausible magnitude.

formulas.name: Dimensional homogeneity
formulas.plain: dimensions(left side) = dimensions(right side)
conditions: Required for any valid physical equation.
checks: Every additive term must have identical dimensions.

formulas.name: Dot product
formulas.plain: A dot B = A B cos(theta)
conditions: Euclidean three-space with a common basis.
checks: Result is a scalar and lies between -AB and AB.

formulas.name: Cross product
formulas.plain: magnitude(A cross B) = A B sin(theta)
conditions: Oriented three-dimensional space.
checks: Direction follows the right-hand rule; result vanishes for parallel vectors.

formulas.name: Projection
formulas.plain: projection of a onto b = (a dot b / b squared) b
conditions: b must be nonzero.
checks: The result is parallel to b.

commonTraps: Adding quantities with different dimensions.
Using degrees inside a calculator set to radians.
Treating vector magnitudes as signed components.
Reporting many digits after an order-of-magnitude estimate.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: One-dimensional kinematics
recognition: Use when motion is confined to one coordinate and the force law is not yet needed; the data describe position, velocity, acceleration, or an area/slope on a motion graph.
keyIdeas: Velocity is the derivative of position; acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
Signed displacement differs from distance traveled.
Constant-acceleration equations are special cases, not definitions.
workflow: Choose the positive direction and origin.
Translate words or graphs into x, v, and a.
Integrate or differentiate unless acceleration is explicitly constant.
Select the equation that omits the unwanted variable.

formulas.name: Kinematic definitions
formulas.plain: v = dx/dt; a = dv/dt = d2x/dt2
conditions: Differentiable one-dimensional motion.
checks: Slope of x(t) is v; slope of v(t) is a.

formulas.name: Integral update
formulas.plain: velocity and position are updated by areas under a(t) and v(t)
conditions: Works for variable acceleration.
checks: Areas carry units of velocity and displacement.

formulas.name: Constant acceleration
formulas.plain: constant-a kinematic equations
conditions: Acceleration constant over the interval; time measured from the initial state.
checks: Reduce to uniform motion when a=0.

commonTraps: Using constant-acceleration formulas when a depends on time or position.
Dropping the sign of gravitational acceleration after choosing axes.
Equating zero velocity with zero acceleration at a turning point.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Two-dimensional, projectile, circular, and polar motion
recognition: Use when position changes in more than one direction, a path is curved, or the radial and transverse directions themselves rotate.
keyIdeas: Treat Cartesian components independently but use a single common time.
Normal acceleration changes direction; tangential acceleration changes speed.
Polar unit vectors rotate, producing extra velocity and acceleration terms.
workflow: Choose Cartesian or polar coordinates to match the geometry.
Write the full vector acceleration before projecting forces.
For projectiles without drag, solve horizontal and vertical components with the same flight time.
Check radial signs and limiting cases such as constant radius.

formulas.name: Vector derivatives
formulas.plain: v = time derivative of r; a = second derivative of r
conditions: In an inertial Cartesian basis or with basis derivatives included.
checks: Each component has units L/T or L/T^2.

formulas.name: Projectile components
formulas.plain: ideal projectile component equations
conditions: Uniform gravity, no drag, flat nonrotating frame.
checks: Horizontal velocity is constant; vertical acceleration is -g.

formulas.name: Circular acceleration
formulas.plain: a = tangential acceleration + v squared/R toward center
conditions: Motion along a smooth path.
checks: Normal term remains when speed is constant.

formulas.name: Polar velocity
formulas.plain: v = rdot r-hat + r phidot phi-hat
conditions: Planar polar coordinates.
checks: For fixed r, speed is r absolute(phidot).

formulas.name: Polar acceleration
formulas.plain: a_r = rddot - r phidot^2; a_phi = r phiddot + 2 rdot phidot
conditions: Planar polar coordinates.
checks: Fixed-radius uniform motion leaves only inward -r omega^2.

formulas.name: Relative velocity
formulas.plain: velocity of A relative C = A relative B + B relative C
conditions: Galilean velocities between nonrelativistic frames.
checks: Order of the subscripts matters.

commonTraps: Using separate flight times for x and y.
Calling v^2/R a new force rather than an acceleration requirement.
Differentiating polar components but not the rotating unit vectors.
Using Galilean velocity addition near light speed.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Newton's laws and free-body modeling
recognition: Use when the question asks for acceleration, force, normal force, tension, or a condition of translational equilibrium and interactions can be listed explicitly.
keyIdeas: A free-body diagram contains forces on one chosen system only.
Newton's third-law partners act on different bodies.
Choose a system boundary that removes unnecessary internal forces.
Force components equal mass times acceleration components only in an inertial frame.
workflow: Choose the system and inertial frame.
Draw every external force with a physical agent.
Choose axes that simplify acceleration or constraints.
Project the vector equation and solve simultaneously.

formulas.name: Newton's second law
formulas.plain: net external force = rate of change of momentum
conditions: Inertial frame; general form permits changing system momentum.
checks: Net force and acceleration point together for constant positive mass.

formulas.name: Constant-mass form
formulas.plain: net external force = mass times acceleration
conditions: Fixed-mass system in an inertial frame.
checks: If acceleration is zero, forces balance vectorially.

formulas.name: Action-reaction pair
formulas.plain: force of A on B = minus force of B on A
conditions: For a mutual interaction pair.
checks: The two forces never belong on the same single-body diagram.

formulas.name: Near-Earth weight
formulas.plain: weight = mass times local gravitational acceleration
conditions: Region small enough that g is nearly uniform.
checks: Weight is not generally equal to normal force.

commonTraps: Drawing ma as a force.
Assuming the normal force equals mg.
Pairing equal and opposite forces that act on the same object.
Writing one scalar equation without defining its positive direction.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Constraints, friction, tension, and circular-force problems
recognition: Use when surfaces, strings, rolling contacts, or prescribed paths couple accelerations and unknown reaction forces.
keyIdeas: Constraint equations are as important as force equations.
Static friction adjusts up to a limit; it is not automatically mu_s N.
Ideal massless strings over frictionless pulleys impose equal tension and a geometric acceleration relation.
The centripetal requirement is the radial sum of real forces.
workflow: Draw separate free-body diagrams for coupled bodies.
Write the geometric constraint and differentiate if needed.
Decide whether contact sticks, slips, or is about to slip.
Project along tangential and normal directions and verify contact forces remain physical.

formulas.name: Coulomb friction
formulas.plain: static friction magnitude <= mu_s N; kinetic friction magnitude = mu_k N
conditions: Dry contact model; kinetic friction opposes relative sliding.
checks: Solve for f_s first, then compare with its maximum.

formulas.name: Radial force balance
formulas.plain: outward-positive radial force sum = -m v squared/R
conditions: Outward radial axis; flip sign if inward is positive.
checks: Only real forces appear on the left in an inertial frame.

formulas.name: Ideal string constraint
formulas.plain: total inextensible-string length is constant

variables.meaning: coordinates of attachment points or pulleys

conditions: Massless, inextensible string without slip.
checks: Differentiate once for velocities and twice for accelerations.

formulas.name: No-slip rolling constraint
formulas.plain: v center = R omega; a center = R alpha
conditions: Pure rolling on a stationary surface; signs depend on coordinate convention.
checks: Point of contact has zero instantaneous velocity relative to surface.

commonTraps: Setting static friction to its maximum before checking.
Assuming connected accelerations are equal without deriving string geometry.
Adding a centrifugal force in an inertial-frame free-body diagram.
Using a_CM=R alpha for slipping motion.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Drag forces and charged-particle motion
recognition: Use when velocity-dependent forces make acceleration nonconstant, or when a magnetic field bends a charged particle without changing its speed.
keyIdeas: Linear drag is analytically exponential; quadratic drag is more realistic at high Reynolds number.
Terminal speed is the stable root of the force balance.
A uniform magnetic field does no work and creates helical or circular motion.
workflow: Choose a signed velocity axis and write the differential equation before substituting magnitudes.
Find equilibrium speed and a natural time or length scale.
Solve the first-order equation or use components/complex notation for magnetic motion.
Check early-time acceleration and long-time terminal behavior.

formulas.name: Linear drag equation
formulas.plain: m dv/dt = mg - b v for downward-positive fall
conditions: One-dimensional motion with drag -b v.
checks: Terminal speed mg/b and time constant m/b.

formulas.name: Linear-drag solution
formulas.plain: v approaches terminal speed exponentially
conditions: Constant g and b with the chosen downward-positive convention.
checks: At t=0 recover v0; at large t recover vt.

formulas.name: Quadratic terminal speed
formulas.plain: terminal speed = sqrt(mg/c)

variables.meaning: coefficient in drag magnitude c v squared

conditions: Vertical fall with force -c v|v| and downward terminal motion.
checks: Larger area or c lowers terminal speed.

formulas.name: Lorentz magnetic force
formulas.plain: magnetic force = q v cross B
conditions: Nonrelativistic point charge in a specified field.
checks: F dot v = 0, so magnetic force changes direction not speed.

formulas.name: Cyclotron motion
formulas.plain: cyclotron angular frequency = |q|B/m; radius = m v_perp/(|q|B)
conditions: Uniform B, no electric field, nonrelativistic motion.
checks: Parallel velocity is unchanged; charge sign sets rotation sense.

commonTraps: Using a positive drag force independent of velocity direction.
Confusing terminal speed with constant acceleration.
Claiming a magnetic field increases kinetic energy.
Using total speed instead of perpendicular speed in the cyclotron radius.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Work, kinetic energy, and power
recognition: Use when forces act through displacement and the requested quantity is speed, stopping distance, work, or rate of energy transfer.
keyIdeas: Net work changes kinetic energy even when individual forces are nonconservative.
Only the component of force along displacement performs instantaneous work.
Power is energy transfer per time, not energy itself.
workflow: Choose the system and endpoints.
Identify forces that do work and integrate if force varies with position.
Apply net-work equals change in kinetic energy.
Check the sign of each contribution and whether the path matters.

formulas.name: Work by a force
formulas.plain: work = line integral of F dot dr
conditions: Force specified along a path.
checks: Perpendicular force contributes zero instantaneous work.

formulas.name: Kinetic energy
formulas.plain: K = one half m v squared
conditions: Nonrelativistic point particle or translational center-of-mass motion.
checks: K is nonnegative and frame-dependent.

formulas.name: Work-energy theorem
formulas.plain: net work = change in kinetic energy

variables.meaning: work by all forces on the chosen particle/system

conditions: Use system bookkeeping consistently.
checks: Negative net work lowers speed.

formulas.name: Power
formulas.plain: power = dW/dt = F dot v
conditions: Force applied at a point moving with velocity v.
checks: Units are energy/time; sign shows input or removal.

commonTraps: Using displacement magnitude rather than a line integral.
Including potential energy and work by the same conservative force twice.
Forgetting that kinetic energy depends on reference frame.
Confusing average and instantaneous power.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Conservative forces, potentials, and effective energy
recognition: Use when forces derive from position, the path is irrelevant, or motion can be inferred from a one-dimensional energy diagram without solving time dependence.
keyIdeas: A conservative force is minus the gradient of potential energy.
Mechanical energy is conserved only when the potential has no explicit time dependence and nonconservative work is absent.
Turning points satisfy E=U_eff; stable equilibria are minima.
Effective potentials absorb constrained or angular kinetic terms into a one-dimensional picture.
workflow: Define the system and zero of potential.
Test whether the force is conservative or isolate nonconservative work.
Write the energy equation before substituting endpoints.
Use E-U to determine allowed regions, speed, and stability.

formulas.name: Force from potential
formulas.plain: F = minus gradient U; in 1D Fx = -dU/dx
conditions: Conservative force represented by a single-valued potential.
checks: Force points downhill in U.

formulas.name: Potential difference
formulas.plain: Delta U = minus work by the conservative force
conditions: Conservative force; result path-independent.
checks: Only potential differences affect dynamics.

formulas.name: Mechanical energy balance
formulas.plain: initial mechanical energy plus nonconservative work = final mechanical energy

variables.meaning: work by nonconservative forces on the system

conditions: Fixed convention for the chosen system.
checks: If W_nc=0, K+U is constant.

formulas.name: Equilibrium and stability
formulas.plain: equilibrium where U prime is zero; stable if U double-prime is positive
conditions: Smooth one-dimensional potential near q0.
checks: A maximum is unstable; flat points require higher-order analysis.

formulas.name: Small-oscillation frequency
formulas.plain: omega squared = curvature of U at equilibrium / effective mass
conditions: Small displacement about a stable equilibrium with quadratic kinetic energy.
checks: Positive curvature gives real frequency.

formulas.name: Radial effective potential
formulas.plain: effective radial potential = central potential + angular-momentum barrier
conditions: Two-body central-force reduction.
checks: Barrier diverges as r approaches zero when ell is nonzero.

commonTraps: Conserving K+U when friction or explicit time dependence is present.
Using F=+gradient U.
Setting U=0 at a physically privileged point when only differences matter.
Calling every stationary point stable.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Momentum, impulse, and collisions
recognition: Use when interactions are short, internal forces are large, or the total external impulse is negligible compared with exchanged momentum.
keyIdeas: Momentum conservation is a vector statement about a chosen system.
Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.
Center-of-momentum coordinates simplify two-body scattering.
Impulse is the area under a force-time curve.
workflow: Choose a system that contains all colliding objects.
Check external impulse during the event.
Write momentum conservation component by component.
Add kinetic-energy conservation or a restitution/energy-loss relation only when justified.

formulas.name: Momentum and impulse
formulas.plain: p = m v; impulse = integral F dt = change in p
conditions: Nonrelativistic fixed-mass particle.
checks: Impulse and momentum have identical units.

formulas.name: System momentum balance
formulas.plain: change in total system momentum = external impulse
conditions: Any chosen system over a time interval.
checks: Internal impulses cancel pairwise for ordinary interactions.

formulas.name: Elastic-collision condition
formulas.plain: total kinetic energy before = total kinetic energy after

variables.meaning: total kinetic energy in one frame

conditions: Elastic collision; combine with momentum conservation.
checks: Do not impose for sticking or deforming collisions.

formulas.name: Coefficient of restitution
formulas.plain: e = relative separation speed / relative approach speed in 1D
conditions: One-dimensional line of impact; 0<=e<=1 for ordinary passive collisions.
checks: e=1 elastic; e=0 objects leave with no relative speed.

commonTraps: Conserving momentum for a subsystem with significant external impulse.
Conserving kinetic energy in every collision.
Using speeds where signed velocity components are required.
Solving a 2D collision with only a scalar momentum equation.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Center of mass and variable-mass systems
familyPatterns: Properties of the Center of Mass
recognition: Use when internal motion is complicated but only gross translation matters, or when mass crosses the system boundary as in a rocket.
keyIdeas: The center of mass responds only to net external force.
Total kinetic energy separates into center-of-mass translation plus motion relative to the center of mass.
For variable mass, momentum flux must be included; blindly writing F=m a is unsafe.
workflow: Define which material belongs to the system at each instant.
Compute the center-of-mass coordinate or total momentum.
Separate internal and external forces.
For rockets, state exhaust velocity relative to the rocket and keep sign conventions explicit.

formulas.name: Center of mass
formulas.plain: R = mass-weighted average position
conditions: Discrete particles; replace sum with integral for a continuum.
checks: R lies within the convex hull for positive masses.

formulas.name: Center-of-mass dynamics
formulas.plain: total mass times COM acceleration = net external force
conditions: Fixed total mass or closed particle system in an inertial frame.
checks: Internal forces do not accelerate the COM.

formulas.name: Kinetic-energy decomposition
formulas.plain: total K = COM translational K + K measured in COM frame

variables.meaning: kinetic energy of motion relative to COM

conditions: Nonrelativistic particles with fixed masses.
checks: Cross terms cancel because sum m_i v'_i = 0.

formulas.name: Ideal rocket equation
formulas.plain: speed increment = exhaust speed times ln(initial mass/final mass)
conditions: No external force over burn or treated separately; constant exhaust speed.
checks: Mass ratio must exceed one for positive speed gain.

formulas.name: Rocket with external force
formulas.plain: m vdot = external force + exhaust relative velocity times mass-loss rate

variables.meaning: velocity of transferred mass relative to rocket
rocket mass rate, negative while losing mass

conditions: Consistent definition of rocket as an open system.
checks: Sign of u_rel mdot should accelerate rocket opposite exhaust.

commonTraps: Using the geometric center for a nonuniform body.
Including internal forces in the COM force sum.
Applying the constant-mass equation directly to a rocket.
Using exhaust speed in the ground frame in the rocket equation.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Angular momentum and torque
recognition: Use when rotation about a point or axis is driven by off-center forces, or when a torque-free symmetry makes angular momentum conserved.
keyIdeas: Angular momentum and torque depend on the chosen origin unless special conditions hold.
The angular impulse changes angular momentum.
For a system, internal central torques cancel and only external torque changes total angular momentum.
workflow: Choose and state an origin that simplifies torques.
Compute lever arms with cross products or perpendicular distances.
Decide whether angular momentum about that origin is conserved.
For impacts followed by rotation, separate collision and subsequent energy stages.

formulas.name: Particle angular momentum
formulas.plain: L about O = r cross p
conditions: Any point particle; specify origin O.
checks: L is perpendicular to the r-p plane.

formulas.name: Torque
formulas.plain: torque about O = r cross F
conditions: Force applied at position r relative to O.
checks: A force through the origin produces zero torque.

formulas.name: Angular-momentum balance
formulas.plain: time rate of total angular momentum = net external torque
conditions: O fixed in an inertial frame, or use the appropriate generalized form.
checks: Zero external torque gives constant vector L.

formulas.name: Angular impulse
formulas.plain: change in angular momentum = angular impulse
conditions: Same origin throughout the interval.
checks: Units are angular momentum.

commonTraps: Using L=I omega for an arbitrary axis/body without checking alignment.
Changing torque origins midway.
Conserving rotational kinetic energy during an inelastic impact.
Using rF instead of rF sin(theta).

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Rigid-body rotation, rolling, and rotational energy
recognition: Use when all points of a body maintain fixed separations and share one angular velocity, especially fixed-axis rotation or rolling without slip.
keyIdeas: Moment of inertia depends on axis, not only on total mass.
For a fixed principal axis, torque, angular acceleration, and angular momentum have scalar analogues.
Rolling kinetic energy includes translation and rotation.
workflow: Choose the rotation axis and compute I about that axis.
Write translation and rotation equations separately if the axis moves.
Apply rolling constraints only when contact does not slip.
Use energy when static friction does no work at the contact point.

formulas.name: Moment of inertia
formulas.plain: I = integral of perpendicular distance squared times dm
conditions: Rigid body about a specified axis.
checks: Units are mass times length squared and I>=0.

formulas.name: Parallel-axis theorem
formulas.plain: I about parallel axis = I through COM + M d squared
conditions: One axis passes through COM and axes are parallel.
checks: Moving away from COM increases I.

formulas.name: Common center-axis moments
formulas.plain: thin hoop MR^2; solid disk or cylinder one-half MR^2; solid sphere two-fifths MR^2; thin rod through center one-twelfth ML^2
conditions: Axes are symmetry axes through the center; rod axis is perpendicular to its length.
checks: Use the parallel-axis theorem for shifted axes; a thin rod about one end has I=ML^2/3.

formulas.name: Fixed-axis rotation
formulas.plain: torque = I alpha; angular momentum = I omega
conditions: Rigid body about a fixed principal axis with constant I.
checks: Not generally valid as a vector equation for arbitrary 3D rotation.

formulas.name: Rotational kinetic energy
formulas.plain: rotational kinetic energy = one half I omega squared

variables.meaning: moment of inertia about instantaneous fixed axis

conditions: Rigid-body rotation about that axis.
checks: Energy is nonnegative.

formulas.name: Rolling kinetic energy
formulas.plain: rolling K = translational COM K + rotational K about COM
conditions: Rigid body; no-slip relation may additionally connect v and omega.
checks: Do not omit either term.

commonTraps: Using a tabulated I for the wrong axis.
Treating static friction as automatically dissipative.
Applying tau=I alpha when I changes or axes are not principal.
Forgetting translational energy of a rolling body.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Inertia tensor and principal axes
recognition: Use when a rigid body rotates about a general three-dimensional axis and angular momentum need not be parallel to angular velocity.
keyIdeas: The inertia tensor is symmetric and diagonal in principal-axis coordinates.
Principal moments are eigenvalues and principal axes are orthogonal eigenvectors for a nondegenerate body.
Rotational energy is a quadratic form in angular velocity.
workflow: Place the origin, usually at the center of mass.
Compute tensor components from the mass distribution.
Diagonalize the symmetric tensor.
Express omega in principal axes before using Euler equations or energy.

formulas.name: Inertia tensor
formulas.plain: I_ij = integral of (r squared delta_ij - x_i x_j) dm
conditions: Rigid mass distribution.
checks: Tensor is real symmetric; diagonal entries are nonnegative.

formulas.name: Angular momentum
formulas.plain: L = inertia tensor times omega
conditions: Rigid body about the tensor origin.
checks: L need not be parallel to omega.

formulas.name: Principal-axis equation
formulas.plain: I tensor times principal vector = principal moment times vector
conditions: Diagonalization of a symmetric inertia tensor.
checks: Orthogonal eigenvectors can be chosen.

formulas.name: Three-dimensional rotational energy
formulas.plain: T = one half omega dot I omega
conditions: Rigid body about the tensor origin.
checks: Positive for any nonzero physical rotation.

commonTraps: Treating I as a scalar in general 3D motion.
Using coordinates not centered at the intended origin.
Forgetting minus signs in off-diagonal products of inertia.
Assuming degeneracy gives a unique principal basis.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Euler equations, gyroscopic precession, and tops
recognition: Use when angular-velocity components are expressed in body-fixed principal axes, especially torque-free tumbling or a rapidly spinning top under gravity.
keyIdeas: Body axes rotate, so component derivatives differ from inertial vector derivatives.
Torque-free rotation about the largest or smallest principal axis is stable; the intermediate-axis rotation is unstable.
Fast-top precession follows from torque changing the direction of angular momentum much more than its magnitude.
workflow: Choose principal body axes and identify I1, I2, I3.
Resolve external torque in that basis.
Write all three coupled Euler equations.
Use energy and angular-momentum invariants for qualitative checks.

formulas.name: Euler equations
formulas.plain: I1 omega1dot + (I3-I2) omega2 omega3 = tau1, with cyclic equations
conditions: Body-fixed principal axes through a fixed point or COM.
checks: For spherical I1=I2=I3, equations reduce to I omegadot = tau.

formulas.name: Vector derivative rule
formulas.plain: inertial derivative = body derivative + omega cross A
conditions: Body frame rotates with angular velocity omega.
checks: Explains the cross-coupling in Euler equations.

formulas.name: Fast-top precession
formulas.plain: precession rate approximately torque/L = M g r /(I3 omega3)
conditions: Rapid symmetric top, weak torque, nearly steady precession.
checks: Faster spin gives slower precession.

formulas.name: Euler-angle angular velocity
formulas.plain: body components of omega in the stated z-x-prime-z-double-prime Euler-angle convention

variables.meaning: precession, nutation, and spin Euler angles in this convention

conditions: The listed component equations depend on the chosen Euler-angle convention; state it before use.
checks: For theta=0, spin and precession contributions add along body axis 3.

formulas.name: Torque-free invariants
formulas.plain: rotational energy and angular-momentum magnitude are conserved
conditions: No external torque, fixed principal moments.
checks: Numerical solutions should preserve both invariants.

commonTraps: Differentiating body components as if axes were inertial.
Assuming L is parallel to omega.
Applying the fast-precession formula to slow or nutating motion.
Calling all principal-axis rotations equally stable.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Static equilibrium and elasticity
recognition: Use when a body has zero translational and angular acceleration, or when loads create small elastic deformations.
keyIdeas: Static equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque.
Choose the torque origin to eliminate unknown forces.
Stress is force per area; strain is fractional deformation.
Linear elastic constants apply only in the small-deformation regime.
workflow: Isolate the body and draw support/contact forces.
Write force balance in independent directions.
Take torques about a convenient point.
Relate stress to strain and verify material/geometry assumptions.

formulas.name: Static equilibrium
formulas.plain: net force = 0 and net torque about O = 0
conditions: Rigid-body translational and angular acceleration both zero.
checks: Torque balance about any origin follows when net force is zero.

formulas.name: Young's modulus
formulas.plain: Young modulus = tensile stress / tensile strain
conditions: Small linear uniaxial deformation.
checks: Strain is dimensionless; Y has pressure units.

formulas.name: Shear modulus
formulas.plain: shear modulus = shear stress / shear strain
conditions: Small linear shear.
checks: G has pressure units.

formulas.name: Bulk modulus
formulas.plain: bulk modulus = -pressure change / fractional volume change
conditions: Small uniform compression.
checks: Compression has negative Delta V, so B is positive.

commonTraps: Using force balance without torque balance.
Counting a support reaction twice.
Confusing stress with force or strain with extension.
Applying Hooke-law elasticity beyond the linear regime.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Newtonian gravitation and spherical bodies
recognition: Use for forces, fields, potentials, or energies caused by mass, especially when spherical symmetry permits shell-theorem shortcuts.
keyIdeas: Gravity is conservative and attractive.
Outside a spherical mass distribution, the field equals that of a point mass at its center.
Inside a spherical shell the field is zero, but the potential is constant and generally nonzero.
Tides depend on field gradients rather than field magnitude alone.
workflow: Exploit symmetry before integrating.
Choose field or potential depending on which superposes more simply.
For spherical interiors, include only enclosed mass in the field.
Check continuity of potential and the far-field point-mass limit.

formulas.name: Newtonian force
formulas.plain: gravitational force = -G m1 m2/r squared in radial direction

variables.meaning: unit vector from source to test mass

conditions: Point masses or nonoverlapping spherical bodies.
checks: Attractive and inverse-square.

formulas.name: Field and potential
formulas.plain: g = -gradient Phi; outside point/sphere Phi = -GM/r
conditions: Zero potential at infinity; outside spherical mass M.
checks: g points inward and scales as 1/r squared.

formulas.name: Potential energy
formulas.plain: two-mass gravitational potential energy = -G m1 m2/r
conditions: Zero at infinite separation.
checks: Bound circular/elliptic systems have negative total energy.

formulas.name: Spherical enclosed-mass field
formulas.plain: radial field = -G enclosed mass/r squared
conditions: Spherically symmetric density.
checks: A uniform-density sphere has g proportional to r inside.

formulas.name: Weak tidal scale
formulas.plain: differential gravity across size ell approximately 2GM ell/r cubed
conditions: ell much smaller than r in a point-mass field.
checks: Tides fall as inverse cube.

commonTraps: Using total mass rather than enclosed mass inside a sphere.
Setting potential to zero inside a shell.
Dropping the negative sign of gravitational potential energy.
Equating strong gravity with strong tides.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Two-body reduction and orbital motion
recognition: Use when two bodies interact through a central force and the relative orbit, period, energy, eccentricity, or transfer maneuver is requested.
keyIdeas: The relative coordinate behaves like one particle of reduced mass in the central potential.
Angular momentum confines motion to a plane.
Inverse-square bound orbits are ellipses; zero/positive energy gives parabolic/hyperbolic escape.
Specific orbital energy and angular momentum often simplify algebra.
workflow: Move to center-of-mass and relative coordinates.
Write conserved energy and angular momentum.
Use the orbit equation or vis-viva relation.
Check bound/unbound sign, periapsis/apoapsis limits, and dimensions.

formulas.name: Reduced mass
formulas.plain: reduced mass = m1 m2/(m1+m2)
conditions: Two-body separation coordinate r=r1-r2.
checks: mu is less than either positive mass.

formulas.name: Kepler orbit
formulas.plain: conic orbit r = p/[1+e cos(phi-phi0)]
conditions: Attractive inverse-square central force.
checks: e<1 ellipse, e=1 parabola, e>1 hyperbola.

formulas.name: Vis-viva equation
formulas.plain: v squared = GM(2/r - 1/a)

variables.meaning: dominant central mass or total mass for relative orbit

conditions: Keplerian two-body orbit.
checks: For circular r=a, v squared=GM/r.

formulas.name: Orbital energy
formulas.plain: bound two-body orbital energy = -GM mu/(2a)
conditions: Elliptic inverse-square orbit.
checks: Larger a is less tightly bound.

formulas.name: Kepler's third law
formulas.plain: period squared = 4 pi squared a cubed/[G total mass]
conditions: Bound two-body inverse-square orbit.
checks: T scales as a^(3/2).

formulas.name: Binet orbit equation
formulas.plain: u double-prime plus u = -mu F(r)/(ell squared u squared), with r=1/u
conditions: Planar central-force motion; prime denotes derivative with respect to phi.
checks: For F=-k/r^2=-k u^2, the right side is the positive constant mu k/ell^2.

formulas.name: Escape speed
formulas.plain: escape speed = sqrt(2GM/r)
conditions: No drag, zero speed at infinity, central mass effectively fixed.
checks: Equals sqrt(2) times circular speed at same r.

commonTraps: Using one body's mass instead of total mass in the relative-period law.
Assuming orbit speed is constant on an ellipse.
Calling e=1 a bound ellipse.
Confusing total orbital energy with potential energy.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Simple harmonic motion and small oscillations
recognition: Use near a stable equilibrium when the restoring force is approximately linear in displacement.
keyIdeas: SHM is the universal leading approximation near a smooth stable equilibrium.
Frequency depends on stiffness-to-inertia ratio, not amplitude in the linear limit.
Position and velocity are quarter-cycle out of phase.
Energy alternates between quadratic kinetic and potential forms.
workflow: Find equilibrium before defining displacement.
Expand the force or potential to leading nonzero order.
Identify the effective mass and stiffness.
Set constants from initial conditions and check energy.

formulas.name: SHM equation
formulas.plain: x double-dot + omega0 squared x = 0
conditions: Linear restoring dynamics without damping or drive.
checks: Acceleration always points toward equilibrium.

formulas.name: SHM solution
formulas.plain: x = A cos(omega0 t + phi)
conditions: Constant omega0.
checks: Maximum speed A omega0 occurs at equilibrium.

formulas.name: Mass-spring frequency
formulas.plain: omega0 = sqrt(k/m); period = 2pi/omega0
conditions: Ideal linear spring and mass.
checks: Stiffer spring raises frequency; heavier mass lowers it.

formulas.name: Small-angle pendulum
formulas.plain: small-angle pendulum omega0 = sqrt(g/length)
conditions: Point bob, massless string, small angle in radians.
checks: Period is independent of bob mass.

formulas.name: Physical pendulum
formulas.plain: physical-pendulum omega0 = sqrt(M g d / I about pivot)
conditions: Rigid body oscillating through small angles about a fixed horizontal pivot.
checks: If mass concentrates at distance d so I_P=Md^2, recover sqrt(g/d).

formulas.name: Torsional oscillator
formulas.plain: torsional frequency = sqrt(torsion constant/moment of inertia)

variables.meaning: moment of inertia about torsion axis

conditions: Linear restoring torque tau=-kappa theta.
checks: Angular stiffness divided by rotational inertia mirrors k/m.

formulas.name: SHM energy
formulas.plain: total SHM energy = one half m v squared + one half k x squared
conditions: Undamped ideal oscillator.
checks: At turning points v=0 and |x|=A.

commonTraps: Measuring x from an unstretched spring rather than equilibrium when gravity acts.
Using sin(theta)=theta for large angles.
Using cyclic frequency f where angular frequency omega is required.
Assuming amplitude-independent period for nonlinear oscillations.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Damped and driven oscillations
recognition: Use when energy loss causes transients or an external periodic force produces a steady-state response.
keyIdeas: The homogeneous solution is the transient; the particular solution is the long-time driven response.
Underdamped motion oscillates within an exponential envelope.
The displacement resonance shifts below the natural frequency when damping is finite.
Quality factor measures narrowness and energy storage relative to loss.
workflow: Normalize the equation and identify omega0, damping rate, and drive frequency.
Classify under-, critical-, or overdamping.
Write transient plus steady-state response.
Check low-frequency, high-frequency, and zero-damping limits.

formulas.name: Driven damped oscillator
formulas.plain: m xddot + b xdot + kx = F0 cos(omega t)
conditions: Linear oscillator with viscous damping and sinusoidal drive.
checks: Every term has force units.

formulas.name: Underdamped transient
formulas.plain: transient decays as exp(-gamma t) at damped frequency
conditions: gamma < omega0.
checks: Envelope decays; omega_d < omega0.

formulas.name: Steady-state amplitude
formulas.plain: steady amplitude = F0/sqrt[(k-m omega squared)^2+(b omega)^2]
conditions: Long-time sinusoidal steady state.
checks: At omega=0, A=F0/k; at large omega, A falls as 1/omega squared.

formulas.name: Phase lag
formulas.plain: tan phase lag = b omega/(k-m omega squared)

variables.meaning: lag of displacement behind force, with quadrant chosen physically

conditions: Sinusoidal steady state.
checks: Lag approaches 0 at low frequency and pi at high frequency.

formulas.name: Quality factor
formulas.plain: Q = m omega0/b = omega0/(2 gamma)
conditions: Weakly damped linear oscillator.
checks: Large Q means slow decay and narrow resonance.

commonTraps: Keeping only the steady state when initial transients are asked.
Using omega0 as the damped frequency.
Ignoring the phase quadrant in arctangent.
Assuming resonance implies infinite amplitude when damping is present.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Fourier decomposition and linear response
recognition: Use when a periodic but nonsinusoidal drive can be decomposed into harmonics and each harmonic passed independently through a linear system.
keyIdeas: Linearity permits superposition of harmonic responses.
Fourier coefficients encode amplitude and phase at discrete harmonics.
Parseval's relation connects mean-square signal strength to coefficient power.
Complex exponentials simplify differentiation; take the real part at the end.
workflow: Identify the period and fundamental frequency.
Use symmetry to eliminate sine or cosine coefficients.
Compute coefficients and apply the transfer function to each harmonic.
Recombine and check convergence or RMS power.

formulas.name: Real Fourier series
formulas.plain: periodic f equals DC plus cosine and sine harmonics
conditions: Piecewise regular periodic function.
checks: Even functions have b_n=0; odd functions have a_n=0.

formulas.name: Fourier coefficients
formulas.plain: coefficients are period-averaged projections onto harmonics
conditions: Same normalization as the listed real series.
checks: Coefficient units match f.

formulas.name: Complex response
formulas.plain: complex displacement amplitude = susceptibility times force amplitude
conditions: Linear damped oscillator under a harmonic component.
checks: Magnitude reproduces the amplitude denominator; argument gives phase.

formulas.name: Parseval relation
formulas.plain: mean square equals sum of harmonic coefficient power
conditions: Real Fourier normalization used above.
checks: Both sides are nonnegative and have units f squared.

commonTraps: Using the wrong coefficient normalization.
Forgetting the DC term.
Dropping phase information when combining responses.
Applying superposition to a nonlinear oscillator.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Traveling waves and energy transport
recognition: Use when a disturbance propagates through a medium and the question concerns speed, wavelength, phase, intensity, or power transport.
keyIdeas: A traveling wave transports energy and momentum without net transport of the medium over a cycle.
The wave speed is set by restoring stiffness divided by inertia density.
Phase velocity links frequency and wavenumber; nondispersive waves preserve shape.
workflow: Identify propagation direction from the phase sign.
Relate wavelength, frequency, and speed.
Differentiate the wave to get element velocity or slope.
Average quadratic energy quantities over a cycle when requested.

formulas.name: Traveling sinusoid
formulas.plain: right-moving wave y = A cos(kx - omega t + phi)
conditions: Monochromatic wave moving in +x with this sign convention.
checks: Constant phase moves toward increasing x.

formulas.name: Wave-speed relation
formulas.plain: phase speed = omega/k = frequency times wavelength
conditions: Single-frequency component.
checks: Units are length/time.

formulas.name: String wave speed
formulas.plain: wave speed on string = sqrt(tension/linear density)
conditions: Small transverse waves on a taut flexible string.
checks: More tension increases speed; more mass density lowers it.

formulas.name: One-dimensional wave equation
formulas.plain: y_xx = (1/v squared) y_tt
conditions: Linear homogeneous nondispersive medium.
checks: Any f(x-vt)+g(x+vt) satisfies it.

formulas.name: Average string power
formulas.plain: average power = one half linear density times wave speed times omega squared A squared
conditions: Sinusoidal small-amplitude wave on a string.
checks: Power scales as amplitude squared and frequency squared.

commonTraps: Confusing element velocity partial y/partial t with propagation speed.
Reading propagation direction from k alone rather than the full phase.
Using mass density instead of linear density for a string.
Using peak rather than cycle-averaged power without stating it.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Standing waves, boundary conditions, and normal modes
recognition: Use when reflections and boundaries select discrete spatial patterns or resonant frequencies.
keyIdeas: Standing waves arise from opposite traveling waves of equal frequency and amplitude.
Boundary conditions quantize allowed wavenumbers.
Normal modes evolve independently only in the linear regime.
Nodes and antinodes refer to spatial amplitude, not permanently stationary material except at nodes.
workflow: State boundary conditions at each end.
Choose sine/cosine spatial form that satisfies one boundary.
Apply the other boundary to quantize k.
Build general motion as a superposition of modes.

formulas.name: Standing-wave form
formulas.plain: standing wave = spatial sine times temporal cosine
conditions: Superposition of equal counterpropagating waves.
checks: Nodes occur where sin(kx)=0.

formulas.name: Fixed-fixed string modes
formulas.plain: fixed-fixed modes: k_n=n pi/L; f_n=n v/(2L)
conditions: Both ends fixed, uniform string.
checks: Fundamental wavelength is 2L.

formulas.name: One-end-closed modes
formulas.plain: closed-open tube frequencies are odd multiples of v/(4L)
conditions: Displacement node at closed end and antinode at open end, ideal end correction ignored.
checks: Only odd harmonics occur.

formulas.name: Beat frequency
formulas.plain: beat frequency = absolute difference of close frequencies
conditions: Linear superposition of two tones with close frequencies.
checks: Carrier oscillates near their average frequency.

commonTraps: Using the fixed-fixed formula for a closed-open tube.
Calling every harmonic a normal mode when boundary conditions differ.
Confusing beat frequency with average pitch.
Forgetting end conditions on pressure versus displacement in air columns.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Sound, interference, Doppler shift, and shocks
recognition: Use when longitudinal pressure waves propagate through a fluid, sources interfere, or source/observer motion changes detected frequency.
keyIdeas: Sound speed is a medium property, not the source speed.
Intensity follows inverse-square spreading for an isotropic point source.
Doppler signs are safest when derived from wavefront spacing and encounter rate.
Supersonic motion creates a Mach cone.
workflow: Identify medium, source, and observer velocities relative to the medium.
Use path differences for interference.
Apply intensity or decibel relations with correct ratios.
For Doppler shift, check whether approach should raise frequency.

formulas.name: Sound speed in fluid
formulas.plain: sound speed = sqrt(bulk modulus/density)
conditions: Small longitudinal waves in a fluid.
checks: Stiffer medium raises speed; denser medium lowers it if B fixed.

formulas.name: Point-source intensity
formulas.plain: intensity = power/(4 pi r squared)
conditions: Far-field isotropic propagation without absorption.
checks: Doubling r quarters intensity.

formulas.name: Sound level
formulas.plain: sound level = 10 log10(I/I0) decibels
conditions: Intensity level definition.
checks: Factor 10 in intensity is +10 dB.

formulas.name: Classical Doppler formula
formulas.plain: observed f = source f times (v+observer toward source)/(v-source toward observer)
conditions: Sound in a stationary medium with stated sign convention and subsonic motions.
checks: Approach raises f prime.

formulas.name: Mach angle
formulas.plain: sin Mach angle = sound speed/source speed = 1/Mach number
conditions: Source speed exceeds sound speed.
checks: Higher Mach number gives narrower cone.

commonTraps: Using source speed as wave speed.
Adding decibel values as if they were intensities.
Memorizing Doppler signs without checking approach/recession.
Applying the subsonic Doppler denominator at or above the wave speed.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Calculus of variations
recognition: Use when the unknown is an entire path or function chosen to extremize an integral functional.
keyIdeas: Stationarity means the first-order change vanishes for allowed endpoint-preserving variations.
The Euler-Lagrange equation is a differential equation for the extremal path.
A stationary path may be a minimum, maximum, or saddle; physical action needs stationarity, not necessarily least numerical value.
workflow: Identify the functional integrand and independent variable.
Specify fixed or free endpoint conditions.
Compute partial derivatives with respect to the function and its derivative.
Solve the Euler-Lagrange equation and test boundary conditions.

formulas.name: Functional
formulas.plain: J of function y = integral F(y,y prime,x) dx
conditions: Admissible differentiable paths with prescribed boundary data.
checks: J is a number assigned to an entire function.

formulas.name: Euler-Lagrange equation
formulas.plain: d/dx(partial F/partial y prime) - partial F/partial y = 0
conditions: Smooth integrand and fixed endpoint variations.
checks: If F has no y dependence, partial F/partial y prime is constant.

formulas.name: Beltrami identity
formulas.plain: F - y prime partial F/partial y prime is constant

variables.meaning: independent variable absent explicitly from F

conditions: F has no explicit x dependence.
checks: First integral lowers differential-equation order.

formulas.name: Multiple coordinates
formulas.plain: Euler-Lagrange equation for each generalized coordinate
conditions: Allowed variations satisfy endpoint and constraint assumptions.
checks: One equation per independent coordinate.

commonTraps: Varying parameters instead of the full path.
Dropping endpoint terms when endpoints are free.
Assuming stationary always means global minimum.
Treating y and y prime as dependent during partial differentiation.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Lagrangian mechanics and constraints
recognition: Use when coordinates are curvilinear, constraints make Cartesian forces cumbersome, or symmetry is more useful than individual constraint forces.
keyIdeas: Generalized coordinates encode configuration, not necessarily lengths or angles with identical units.
For ideal holonomic constraints, reaction forces can disappear from the virtual-work equations.
The Lagrangian is usually T-U in an inertial frame, but generalized potentials can include velocity dependence.
Constraint multipliers recover unknown reaction forces when needed.
workflow: Count degrees of freedom and choose independent coordinates.
Write all positions in those coordinates before differentiating.
Build T and U, then L=T-U.
Apply one Euler-Lagrange equation per coordinate and interpret conserved generalized momenta.

formulas.name: Lagrange equations
formulas.plain: d/dt(partial L/partial qdot_i) - partial L/partial q_i = nonconservative generalized force
conditions: Independent generalized coordinates; ideal constraints handled in coordinates.
checks: Dimensions of each equation match generalized force units.

formulas.name: Generalized force
formulas.plain: Q_i = sum F_a dot partial r_a/partial q_i
conditions: Virtual displacement compatible with coordinate q_i.
checks: If q_i is an angle, Q_i has torque units.

formulas.name: Holonomic constraint
formulas.plain: constraint function f_alpha(q,t)=0
conditions: Constraint expressible as coordinate/time equation.
checks: Independent constraints reduce degrees of freedom one each.

formulas.name: Multiplier equations
formulas.plain: Euler-Lagrange with constraint forces from lambda times constraint gradients

variables.meaning: Lagrange multiplier related to reaction force

conditions: Holonomic constraints retained rather than eliminated.
checks: Solve motion and multipliers together with f_alpha=0.

commonTraps: Using dependent generalized coordinates as independent.
Forgetting coordinate dependence of kinetic energy.
Writing L=U-T.
Assuming generalized momentum always equals ordinary linear momentum.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Cyclic coordinates and conservation laws
recognition: Use when the Lagrangian has a coordinate symmetry or explicit time independence, allowing a conserved quantity before solving the equations of motion.
keyIdeas: If L lacks a coordinate, its conjugate momentum is conserved.
If L lacks explicit time, the energy function is conserved.
A conserved canonical momentum can differ from mechanical momentum in velocity-dependent potentials.
Symmetry recognition is often the fastest route through a qual problem.
workflow: Inspect L before differentiating.
Identify absent coordinates and explicit time dependence.
Write the associated conserved quantity.
Use it to reduce the order or dimension of the remaining equations.

formulas.name: Canonical momentum
formulas.plain: canonical momentum p_i = partial L/partial qdot_i
conditions: Differentiable Lagrangian.
checks: Its units depend on q_i.

formulas.name: Cyclic-coordinate conservation
formulas.plain: if L does not depend on q_i, conjugate momentum is constant
conditions: No nonconservative generalized force in q_i.
checks: Use the actual L, not a coordinate-free verbal claim.

formulas.name: Energy function
formulas.plain: Lagrangian energy function = sum qdot_i p_i - L

variables.meaning: conserved energy function when L has no explicit time

conditions: L has no explicit t and equations hold.
checks: For ordinary T quadratic in velocities and L=T-U, E_L=T+U.

formulas.name: Energy evolution
formulas.plain: time derivative of energy function = minus explicit time derivative of L
conditions: Along Euler-Lagrange motion without added nonconservative forces.
checks: Explicit time independence gives conservation.

formulas.name: Charged-particle Lagrangian
formulas.plain: L = one-half m v squared - q scalar potential + q vector potential dot v
conditions: Nonrelativistic particle in prescribed electromagnetic potentials.
checks: Euler-Lagrange equations give q(E+v cross B).

formulas.name: Electromagnetic canonical momentum
formulas.plain: canonical momentum = mechanical momentum + q A
conditions: Same electromagnetic Lagrangian and gauge convention.
checks: Canonical momentum is gauge-dependent; mechanical momentum m v is not.

commonTraps: Calling q_i conserved instead of p_i.
Assuming Hamiltonian equals mechanical energy for every velocity-dependent L.
Missing a symmetry hidden by a poor coordinate choice.
Conserving energy when L depends explicitly on time.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Accelerating and rotating frames
recognition: Use when observations are made from a frame with translational acceleration or angular velocity relative to an inertial frame.
keyIdeas: Apparent forces arise from frame acceleration, not new interactions.
Coriolis force depends on velocity in the rotating frame and does no work there.
Centrifugal effects can be derived from a potential for constant rotation.
Euler force appears only when frame angular velocity changes.
workflow: Define inertial and rotating frames plus origin acceleration and omega.
Transform acceleration completely.
Move frame-acceleration terms to the force side if using apparent forces.
Check signs with simple cases: object at rest in rotating frame or free inertial motion.

formulas.name: Derivative transformation
formulas.plain: inertial derivative = rotating derivative + Omega cross A
conditions: Same vector described in frames I and R.
checks: Apply twice to position for acceleration.

formulas.name: Acceleration transformation
formulas.plain: inertial acceleration = origin + relative + Coriolis + Euler + centripetal frame terms
conditions: General translating and rotating frame.
checks: All extra terms have acceleration units.

formulas.name: Coriolis apparent force
formulas.plain: Coriolis force = -2m Omega cross relative velocity
conditions: Equation of motion written in rotating frame.
checks: Force is perpendicular to v_R and does no instantaneous work.

formulas.name: Centrifugal apparent force
formulas.plain: centrifugal force = -m Omega cross (Omega cross r)
conditions: Rotating-frame equation; for constant Omega it points away from axis.
checks: Magnitude m Omega squared times perpendicular distance.

formulas.name: Euler apparent force
formulas.plain: Euler force = -m Omegadot cross r
conditions: Nonuniformly rotating frame.
checks: Vanishes for constant rotation rate.

formulas.name: Centrifugal potential
formulas.plain: centrifugal potential = -one-half m times squared distance-speed Omega cross r
conditions: Constant Omega; combine with other potentials in the rotating frame.
checks: Minus its gradient gives outward centrifugal force.

formulas.name: Foucault precession
formulas.plain: Foucault precession rate relative to Earth = Earth rotation rate times sin(latitude)
conditions: Small-amplitude long pendulum; local vertical approximation; sign depends on hemisphere convention.
checks: Zero at equator and one sidereal rotation per day at a pole.

commonTraps: Mixing inertial-frame and rotating-frame velocities.
Forgetting the factor of two in Coriolis force.
Using centrifugal force in an inertial-frame diagram.
Omitting the Euler term when rotation rate changes.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Hamiltonian mechanics and phase space
recognition: Use when phase-space flow, canonical variables, conserved Hamiltonian, or a first-order formulation is requested.
keyIdeas: The Hamiltonian is the Legendre transform of the Lagrangian with respect to velocities.
Hamilton's equations replace n second-order equations with 2n first-order equations.
Phase-space flow preserves volume for Hamiltonian dynamics.
H equals total energy for common time-independent natural Lagrangians, but not automatically for every system.
workflow: Compute canonical momenta and invert for qdot in terms of q,p.
Form H=sum p qdot-L.
Apply Hamilton's equations.
Use conserved H, cyclic coordinates, and phase portraits to analyze motion.

formulas.name: Legendre transform
formulas.plain: H = sum p_i qdot_i - L, after eliminating qdot
conditions: Velocity-momentum map is invertible for a regular Lagrangian.
checks: Final H must be expressed in q,p,t, not qdot.

formulas.name: Hamilton's equations
formulas.latex: \dot q_i=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i},\qquad\dot p_i=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}
formulas.plain: qdot_i = partial H/partial p_i; pdot_i = -partial H/partial q_i
conditions: Canonical variables.
checks: For H=p squared/(2m)+U, recover qdot=p/m and pdot=-U prime.

formulas.name: Hamiltonian evolution
formulas.plain: along Hamiltonian motion, total dH/dt equals explicit partial H/partial t
conditions: No non-Hamiltonian forcing.
checks: No explicit time dependence implies H conserved.

formulas.name: Poisson bracket
formulas.plain: Poisson bracket = sum(f_q g_p - f_p g_q)
conditions: Canonical coordinates.
checks: Antisymmetric: {f,g}=-{g,f}.

formulas.name: Observable evolution
formulas.plain: time change of f = Poisson bracket with H + explicit time derivative
conditions: Hamiltonian motion.
checks: For f=H, bracket vanishes.

formulas.name: Liouville theorem
formulas.plain: phase-space flow has zero divergence
conditions: Hamiltonian flow in canonical coordinates.
checks: Fine-grained phase-space volume is preserved.

commonTraps: Leaving velocities in the final Hamiltonian.
Missing the minus sign in pdot.
Assuming H always equals T+U.
Interpreting Liouville's theorem as conservation of ordinary spatial volume.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Special-relativistic kinematics
recognition: Use when events are compared between inertial frames at appreciable fractions of light speed, and simultaneity or invariant intervals matter.
keyIdeas: All inertial observers agree on c and the spacetime interval, not on space and time separately.
Proper time belongs to one clock passing through both events.
Proper length is measured in the object's rest frame.
Relativity of simultaneity is essential; time dilation alone cannot solve every geometry.
workflow: Define frames, event coordinates, and relative velocity direction.
Find the invariant interval and identify timelike, spacelike, or lightlike separation.
Apply the Lorentz transformation with a consistent sign convention.
Check the low-speed limit and that no massive result exceeds c.

formulas.name: Lorentz factor
formulas.plain: gamma = 1/sqrt(1-v squared/c squared)
checks: gamma>=1 and approaches 1 at low speed.

formulas.name: Lorentz transformation
formulas.plain: x prime = gamma(x-vt); t prime = gamma(t-vx/c squared)
conditions: Standard configuration; y and z unchanged.
checks: A light ray x=ct also satisfies x'=ct'.

formulas.name: Invariant interval
formulas.plain: c squared proper-time squared = c squared time separation squared - spatial separation squared
conditions: Metric signature +---.
checks: Same value in every inertial frame.

formulas.name: Time dilation
formulas.plain: coordinate time = gamma times proper time

variables.meaning: time on one clock present at both events

conditions: Events occur at same place in the clock's rest frame.
checks: Coordinate interval is no shorter than proper time.

formulas.name: Length contraction
formulas.plain: moving length = proper length/gamma
conditions: Endpoints measured simultaneously in observer frame along motion.
checks: Only the parallel dimension contracts.

formulas.name: Velocity addition
formulas.plain: u prime = (u-v)/(1-u v/c squared)
conditions: Collinear standard frames.
checks: If u_x=c, u'_x=c; low-speed limit is u-v.

formulas.name: Transverse velocity transformation
formulas.plain: transverse velocity in S prime = u_y/[gamma(1-u_x v/c squared)]
conditions: Standard Lorentz boost along x.
checks: Transverse components are not unchanged because time also transforms.

formulas.name: Relativistic longitudinal Doppler
formulas.plain: approaching observed frequency = source frequency sqrt[(1+beta)/(1-beta)]

variables.meaning: positive approach speed/c for this convention

conditions: Source and observer in inertial collinear motion in vacuum.
checks: Approach blueshifts; recession uses inverse factor.

commonTraps: Using time dilation without identifying the proper-time clock.
Using length contraction without simultaneity.
Mixing sign conventions between transformation and velocity addition.
Adding relativistic velocities with the Galilean rule.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Four-momentum, relativistic energy, and collisions
recognition: Use for high-speed particle energy, thresholds, decays, or collisions where Newtonian momentum and kinetic energy are invalid.
keyIdeas: Energy and momentum form a conserved four-vector.
Invariant mass provides a frame-independent collision equation.
Photons have zero rest mass but nonzero energy and momentum.
Center-of-momentum frames simplify threshold and decay problems.
workflow: List each particle's four-momentum and invariant mass.
Conserve total four-momentum.
Square the total to form invariant relations before solving components.
Check rest, ultrarelativistic, and low-speed limits.

formulas.name: Relativistic momentum and energy
formulas.plain: p = gamma m v; total energy = gamma m c squared
conditions: Massive particle.
checks: At rest E=mc squared; at low speed E approximately mc squared + one half mv squared.

formulas.name: Energy-momentum invariant
formulas.plain: E squared = p squared c squared + m squared c to fourth
conditions: Free particle with invariant mass m.
checks: For photon m=0, E=pc.

formulas.name: Four-momentum
formulas.plain: four-momentum = (energy/c, three-momentum)
conditions: Metric/sign convention stated consistently.
checks: Minkowski norm is m squared c squared.

formulas.name: Four-momentum conservation
formulas.plain: total incoming four-momentum = total outgoing four-momentum
conditions: Isolated collision or decay.
checks: Simultaneously conserves energy and all momentum components.

formulas.name: Invariant mass of a system
formulas.plain: system invariant mass squared c fourth = total energy squared - c squared total momentum squared
conditions: Total four-momentum of selected system.
checks: In COM frame P_tot=0 and E_tot=Mc squared.

formulas.name: Photon momentum
formulas.plain: photon energy = p c = h f
conditions: Photon in vacuum.
checks: Higher frequency means larger momentum despite zero rest mass.

formulas.name: Relativistic three-force
formulas.plain: relativistic force = time derivative of relativistic momentum
conditions: Force measured in a specified inertial frame.
checks: In general F is not m times acceleration; parallel and perpendicular responses differ.

formulas.name: Four-force
formulas.plain: four-force = derivative of four-momentum with proper time = gamma(power/c, three-force)
conditions: Massive particle parameterized by proper time.
checks: Four-force is orthogonal to four-velocity for constant invariant mass.

formulas.name: Rank-two tensor transformation
formulas.plain: a rank-two tensor transforms with one Lorentz matrix for each index
conditions: Contravariant rank-two tensor; index placement controls inverse/metric factors.
checks: Contracted scalar quantities remain invariant.

formulas.name: Electromagnetic field boost
formulas.plain: parallel E and B are unchanged; perpendicular fields mix under a boost

variables.meaning: velocity of primed frame relative to unprimed frame under this convention

conditions: Standard inertial boost; SI units; signs reverse if boost convention reverses.
checks: Electric and magnetic fields are frame-dependent parts of one field tensor.

commonTraps: Conserving Newtonian kinetic energy at relativistic speed.
Calling gamma m the invariant mass.
Assigning zero momentum to a photon because m=0.
Applying four-momentum conservation to an open subsystem.

topics.subject: Classical Mechanics
topics.title: Integrated classical-mechanics modeling
recognition: Use for imported problem titles that do not reveal one clean family. The task is to classify the system before selecting equations.
keyIdeas: A correct model choice is more valuable than immediate algebra.
Conservation laws require system and interval choices.
Constraint, force, and energy descriptions must agree when their assumptions overlap.
A solution is incomplete without units, signs, and limiting-case checks.
workflow: Sketch the system, events, and coordinate choices.
State assumptions and identify knowns/unknowns.
Choose a primary method: forces, energy, momentum, angular momentum, Lagrangian, or Hamiltonian.
Solve symbolically first when possible.
Check dimensions, limiting cases, and physical admissibility.

formulas.name: Model-selection ledger
formulas.plain: system + interval + symmetry + constraints determine the equations
conditions: All multi-concept problems.
checks: Every conservation claim names what is conserved and why.

formulas.name: Dimensional check
formulas.plain: dimensions of answer must equal dimensions of requested quantity
conditions: Always.
checks: Also inspect sign, direction, domain, and scale.

commonTraps: Equation hunting from visible numbers.
Changing the system between equations without updating external work/impulse.
Substituting numbers before structure is clear.
Accepting an algebraic root that violates geometry or conservation.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Vector calculus, coordinates, and distributions
recognition: Use this toolkit when the task asks you to convert between local and global field statements, choose coordinates, or handle a point source.
keyIdeas: Gradient points toward fastest scalar increase; divergence measures local source strength; curl measures local circulation.
Integral theorems turn a volume or surface statement into a boundary statement.
Choose coordinates from symmetry before differentiating or integrating.
workflow: Identify scalar, vector, and integration domains.
Exploit symmetry and select Cartesian, cylindrical, or spherical coordinates.
Apply the appropriate theorem and check orientation of normals or contours.
Test the result away from singularities and include delta functions at point sources.

formulas.name: Gradient, divergence, and curl
formulas.plain: grad f, div A, curl A
conditions: Use the coordinate-system form of each operator.
checks: grad f has units f/length; div A has units A/length; curl direction follows the right-hand rule.

formulas.name: Divergence theorem
formulas.plain: volume integral of div A = outward flux through the boundary
conditions: A is sufficiently smooth inside V except for explicitly treated singularities.
checks: Both sides have units A times area.

formulas.name: Stokes theorem
formulas.latex: \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf A)\cdot d\mathbf a=\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf A\cdot d\mathbf l
formulas.plain: curl flux through S = circulation around its boundary
conditions: The contour orientation must be consistent with the surface normal.
checks: Reverse the normal and both sides change sign.

formulas.name: Point-source identity
formulas.plain: divergence of radial inverse-square field is zero away from the origin but integrates to 4 pi
conditions: Distributional identity including the origin.
checks: Flux through every sphere enclosing the origin is 4 pi.

commonTraps: Using Cartesian operator formulas in spherical coordinates.
Dropping the outward-normal sign.
Claiming an inverse-square field has zero divergence everywhere because it is zero for r greater than zero.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Charge, Coulomb force, and electric-field superposition
recognition: Use direct superposition when the source geometry lacks enough symmetry for Gauss's law to determine the field.
keyIdeas: The field is force per unit positive test charge and is independent of the test charge.
Fields add vectorially; charge contributions add linearly.
Far from a localized distribution, the lowest nonzero multipole controls the field.
workflow: Sketch source and field point and define the separation vector from source to field point.
Choose dq as lambda dl, sigma da, or rho d tau.
Use symmetry to cancel components before integrating.
Check direction, inverse-distance behavior, and limiting cases.

formulas.name: Coulomb force
formulas.plain: F12 = k q1 q2 rhat12 / r12^2
conditions: Point charges in vacuum electrostatics.
checks: Like charges repel; force scales as inverse distance squared.

formulas.name: Field of a continuous charge distribution
formulas.latex: \mathbf E(\mathbf r)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int \rho(\mathbf r')\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}\,d\tau'
formulas.plain: E(r) = k integral rho(r') R vector / R^3 d tau'
conditions: Replace rho d tau by lambda dl or sigma da for line or surface charge.
checks: The separation vector points from source to field point.

formulas.name: Electric force
formulas.plain: F = q E
conditions: Exclude the charge's singular self-field.
checks: A negative charge accelerates opposite E.

commonTraps: Using a scalar sum for vector fields.
Reversing source and field points in the separation vector.
Applying Gauss's law as an algebraic shortcut without sufficient symmetry.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Electric flux, Gauss's law, and conductors
familyPatterns: Surface Charge and the Force on a Conductor
Field of a uniformly charged solid cylinder
recognition: Use Gauss's law to calculate E only when symmetry makes the normal field constant or zero on chosen pieces of a closed surface.
keyIdeas: Flux counts the signed field crossing a closed surface, not field lying along it.
Electrostatic conductors have zero interior field and constant potential.
A surface charge creates a jump in the normal electric field.
workflow: Identify planar, cylindrical, or spherical symmetry.
Choose a closed Gaussian surface aligned with the symmetry.
Compute enclosed charge, not total charge in the universe.
Apply boundary conditions and verify inside/outside limits.

formulas.name: Gauss's law
formulas.plain: closed electric flux = enclosed charge / epsilon0
conditions: Always true; algebraically useful for highly symmetric fields.
checks: Only enclosed charge appears on the right, though outside charges can affect E locally.

formulas.name: Differential Gauss law
formulas.plain: div E = rho / epsilon0
conditions: Distributional form includes surface and point sources.
checks: In charge-free space div E = 0, not necessarily E = 0.

formulas.name: Electrostatic boundary jump
formulas.latex: (\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\sigma/\epsilon_0,\qquad (\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)\times\hat{\mathbf n}=0
formulas.plain: normal E jumps by sigma/epsilon0; tangential E is continuous
conditions: Electrostatic interface.
checks: For a conductor surface, E just outside is sigma n / epsilon0.

formulas.name: Electrostatic pressure on a conductor
formulas.plain: outward force per area = epsilon0 Eout^2 / 2
conditions: Conductor in electrostatic equilibrium with vacuum outside.
checks: Use the average field across the sheet to avoid self-force double counting.

commonTraps: Using an open surface in Gauss's law.
Counting charge outside the Gaussian surface.
Assuming zero enclosed charge means zero field.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Electric potential, work, energy, and capacitance
familyPatterns: Electrostatic work and energy of charge and field configurations
recognition: Use potential when the field is conservative, when energy or voltage is requested, or when scalar superposition is simpler than vector superposition.
keyIdeas: Potential differences are physical; the zero of potential is conventional.
Electrostatic work is path independent.
Field energy and source-assembly energy are equivalent descriptions when self-energy is treated consistently.
workflow: Choose a convenient potential reference.
Integrate E along any convenient path or integrate source charge directly.
Differentiate V to recover E when needed.
For capacitors, identify what remains fixed: charge, voltage, or neither.

formulas.name: Potential difference and field
formulas.latex: V(b)-V(a)=-\int_a^b\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l,\qquad \mathbf E=-\nabla V
formulas.plain: Delta V = - line integral E dot dl; E = -grad V
conditions: Electrostatic or otherwise curl-free E in the region.
checks: E points downhill in V.

formulas.name: Potential from charge
formulas.plain: V(r) = k integral rho(r') / R d tau'
conditions: Reference V = 0 at infinity for a localized distribution.
checks: Potential scales as charge over distance for a net charge.

formulas.name: Electrostatic energy
formulas.plain: U = one-half integral rho V = epsilon0/2 integral E squared
conditions: The field form includes all space; point-charge self-energies require care.
checks: Field-energy density in vacuum is nonnegative.

formulas.name: Capacitance and stored energy
formulas.latex: C=Q/\Delta V,\qquad U=Q^2/(2C)=\tfrac12 C(\Delta V)^2=\tfrac12Q\Delta V
formulas.plain: C = Q/Delta V; U = Q^2/(2C) = C DeltaV^2/2

variables.meaning: magnitude of charge on either conductor

conditions: Linear capacitor.
checks: Capacitance depends on geometry and material, not on Q for a linear dielectric.

commonTraps: Forgetting the minus sign between E and grad V.
Using total rather than potential difference in C = Q/Delta V.
Differentiating energy at fixed Q when a battery actually fixes V, or vice versa.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Poisson and Laplace equations, images, separation, and uniqueness
recognition: Use a boundary-value method when conductor shapes or specified boundary data define the problem more naturally than the source integral.
keyIdeas: Laplace solutions have no interior maxima or minima in charge-free regions.
Uniqueness lets a guessed solution become a proof once the differential equation and boundary data are satisfied.
Image charges replace conductors only inside the permitted physical region.
workflow: Partition space into regions and identify rho and boundary data.
Choose images, separation of variables, or Green-function machinery from the geometry.
Solve for constants from all boundary conditions.
Differentiate V, then check the conductor surfaces and asymptotic behavior.

formulas.name: Poisson and Laplace equations
formulas.plain: Laplacian V = -rho/epsilon0; equals zero in charge-free space
conditions: Electrostatics.
checks: A charge-free solution cannot have an isolated interior extremum.

formulas.name: Green's first identity
formulas.plain: volume integral phi Laplacian psi plus grad products equals boundary integral phi normal-derivative psi
conditions: Fields and boundary are sufficiently regular.
checks: Derived by applying the divergence theorem to phi grad psi.

formulas.name: Separated Cartesian Laplace equation
formulas.plain: assume product solution; the three normalized second derivatives sum to zero
conditions: Cartesian separable geometry and compatible boundary conditions.
checks: Separation constants must sum to zero and dimensions match inverse length squared.

commonTraps: Treating image charges as physical charges in the conductor region.
Satisfying only part of the boundary.
Keeping separated modes that violate regularity or asymptotic conditions.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Electric dipoles and multipole expansion
recognition: Use a multipole expansion far from a localized charge distribution, or use dipole mechanics for separated opposite charges in a slowly varying field.
keyIdeas: At large distance, the first nonzero multipole dominates.
The dipole moment is origin independent only when total charge is zero.
A uniform field gives a dipole torque but no net force; a gradient can give a force.
workflow: Compare observation distance with source size.
Compute total charge; if zero, compute p.
Retain only the needed order in source-size over distance.
Check angular dependence and far-field power law.

formulas.name: Electric dipole moment
formulas.plain: p = integral r' rho d tau'

variables.meaning: source position relative to chosen origin

conditions: For point charges, replace the integral by sum qi ri.
checks: Units are charge times length.

formulas.name: Far electric potential
formulas.plain: V far away = k times [Q/r + p dot rhat/r^2 + higher multipoles]

variables.meaning: distance much larger than source size

conditions: Localized source with r much greater than source extent.
checks: Each successive term falls by another power of r.

formulas.name: Dipole torque and energy
formulas.plain: tau = p cross E; U = -p dot E
conditions: Dipole size is small compared with the field-variation scale.
checks: Minimum energy has p aligned with E.

commonTraps: Using the dipole approximation too close to the source.
Forgetting the monopole term when total charge is nonzero.
Assuming a uniform field produces a net dipole force.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Capacitor networks and dielectric response
recognition: Use network rules for lumped capacitors and field methods when geometry or dielectric filling matters.
keyIdeas: Parallel capacitors share voltage; series capacitors carry equal-magnitude charge in a simple chain.
A dielectric reduces the field made by a given free charge.
Mechanical conclusions depend on whether Q or V is held fixed.
workflow: Mark shared nodes to identify series or parallel connections.
Reduce the network or solve node voltages.
For a dielectric insertion, state whether the capacitor is isolated or battery-connected.
Check that equivalent capacitance grows in parallel and shrinks in series.

formulas.name: Ideal parallel-plate capacitance
formulas.plain: C = epsilon A / d
conditions: Negligible fringing and uniform filling.
checks: Larger area or permittivity increases C; larger separation decreases C.

formulas.name: Capacitor combinations
formulas.plain: parallel capacitances add; reciprocal capacitances add in series
conditions: Ideal lumped capacitors.
checks: Series equivalent is smaller than the smallest member; parallel equivalent is larger than the largest.

commonTraps: Using resistor series rules for capacitors.
