Assuming both Q and V stay fixed while geometry changes.
Ignoring fringing outside the ideal-plate limit.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Polarization, bound charge, D, and linear dielectrics
recognition: Use P and D to separate material response from free charge in matter.
keyIdeas: Polarization is dipole moment per volume.
Spatial variation of P produces bound volume charge; termination of P produces bound surface charge.
D is useful because its divergence tracks free charge, but D is not generally determined by free charge alone without symmetry.
workflow: Identify free charge and constitutive law.
Find P from microscopic information or P = epsilon0 chi_e E.
Compute bound charges or use D with symmetry.
Apply interface conditions to solve for fields.

formulas.name: Bound charge from polarization
formulas.plain: rho_bound = -div P; sigma_bound = P dot outward normal
conditions: Macroscopic polarization description.
checks: Uniform P has no volume bound charge but can have surface charge.

formulas.name: Electric displacement
formulas.plain: D = epsilon0 E + P; div D = free charge density
conditions: Macroscopic matter; no linearity assumption needed for the definition.
checks: D normal jumps by free surface charge.

formulas.name: Linear dielectric
formulas.plain: P = epsilon0 chi_e E; D = epsilon E
conditions: Linear, isotropic, homogeneous material for scalar epsilon.
checks: Vacuum has chi_e = 0 and epsilon = epsilon0.

commonTraps: Calling bound charge free charge.
Using D = epsilon E in nonlinear or anisotropic matter without justification.
Assuming curl D is zero in electrostatics.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Current density, resistance, emf, and electric power
recognition: Use transport relations when charge moves through matter and the question asks for current, resistance, power, or local current density.
keyIdeas: Current is charge flow rate through a surface; J is its local vector form.
Ohm's law can be local or lumped and requires an appropriate material regime.
An ideal emf source supplies energy per unit charge; emf is not itself a force.
workflow: Choose a surface and current direction.
Relate J to carrier motion or E.
Convert local geometry to R when uniform.
Track signs and energy conversion with P = IV.

formulas.name: Current and current density
formulas.latex: I=\int_S\mathbf J\cdot d\mathbf a,\qquad \mathbf J=nq\mathbf v_d
formulas.plain: I = surface integral J dot da; J = n q drift velocity
conditions: Single carrier species for J = n q vd; sum over species otherwise.
checks: Conventional current follows positive charge motion.

formulas.name: Ohmic transport
formulas.plain: J = conductivity times E; R = resistivity L/A; V = I R
conditions: Linear ohmic material; R formula assumes uniform geometry.
checks: Longer or thinner wire has larger R.

formulas.name: Electrical power
formulas.plain: P = I V = I squared R = V squared/R; local power density = J dot E
conditions: The alternative lumped forms use V = IR.
checks: Dissipative resistor power is nonnegative under the passive sign convention.

commonTraps: Confusing electron drift direction with conventional current.
Using R = rho L/A for varying cross-section without integrating.
Calling emf a mechanical force or a terminal voltage under all load conditions.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: DC networks, Kirchhoff rules, and RC transients
recognition: Use node and loop equations when a circuit cannot be reduced by simple series-parallel combinations; use a first-order transient for one independent capacitor state.
keyIdeas: Kirchhoff's junction rule is charge conservation; the loop rule is energy conservation for lumped quasistatic circuits.
A capacitor voltage cannot jump without an impulse current.
The time constant determines the approach to the long-time state, not the final value itself.
workflow: Label currents and node voltages consistently.
Find the t = 0+ and t -> infinity limits.
Reduce the network seen by the capacitor to its Thevenin resistance if useful.
Solve and test the initial value and long-time limit.

formulas.name: Kirchhoff rules
formulas.plain: signed currents at a node sum to zero; signed voltage changes around a loop sum to zero

variables.meaning: element voltage change along loop direction

conditions: Lumped quasistatic circuit; include induced emf separately when magnetic flux changes.
checks: A negative solved current simply means the actual direction is opposite the guess.

formulas.name: RC charging and discharging
formulas.plain: capacitor voltage = final value + (initial - final) exp[-t/(Rth C)]

variables.meaning: resistance seen by the capacitor with independent sources deactivated

conditions: Linear first-order circuit with one effective capacitor state.
checks: At t = 0 the expression gives Vi; at long time it gives Vf.

formulas.name: Resistor combinations
formulas.plain: series resistances add; reciprocal resistances add in parallel
conditions: Ideal lumped resistors.
checks: Parallel equivalent is smaller than the smallest branch resistance.

commonTraps: Treating elements as series merely because they are drawn next to each other.
Assuming a capacitor is always open; that is only the DC steady-state limit.
Changing capacitor voltage discontinuously at switching.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Lorentz force, charged-particle motion, and magnetic torque
recognition: Use the Lorentz force for individual charges and its current-element form for wires, loops, and magnetic dipoles.
keyIdeas: A magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity and does no work on a point charge.
Uniform B bends perpendicular motion into a circle while parallel motion remains uniform.
A current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole when the field varies little across it.
workflow: Split velocity into components parallel and perpendicular to B.
Use q v cross B and include the sign of q after the right-hand rule.
For extended currents, integrate d l cross B or use m cross B in the dipole limit.
Check that magnetic force is perpendicular to motion and power is zero.

formulas.name: Lorentz force
formulas.plain: F = q times (E + v cross B)
conditions: Classical point-particle force law.
checks: Magnetic contribution vanishes for v parallel B and is reversed for negative q.

formulas.name: Cyclotron motion
formulas.plain: Larmor radius = m v_perp/(absolute q B); cyclotron angular frequency = absolute q B/m
conditions: Uniform B, nonrelativistic motion, negligible electric field.
checks: Faster or heavier particles have larger radius; frequency is independent of speed.

formulas.name: Force on current and magnetic dipole
formulas.latex: d\mathbf F=I\,d\mathbf l\times\mathbf B,\qquad \mathbf m=I\mathbf a,\qquad \boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf m\times\mathbf B
formulas.plain: dF = I dl cross B; magnetic moment = I area vector; torque = m cross B
conditions: Dipole torque form assumes a small loop in a nearly uniform B.
checks: Stable orientation has m aligned with B.

formulas.name: Magnetic dipole energy
formulas.plain: U = -m dot B
conditions: Localized permanent current loop or dipole in an external field.
checks: Energy is minimized when m and B align.

commonTraps: Forgetting the charge sign after using the right-hand rule.
Claiming B changes a particle's speed.
Using the dipole approximation in a strongly nonuniform field without a gradient-force correction.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Biot-Savart law, Ampere's law, and steady currents
recognition: Use Biot-Savart for general steady-current geometry and Ampere's law for sufficiently symmetric magnetostatic fields.
keyIdeas: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end.
Ampere's law is always true in magnetostatics but only directly calculates B when symmetry fixes the field on the loop.
Steady currents satisfy div J = 0.
workflow: Identify current path or volume current density.
Choose Biot-Savart unless an Amperian loop has constant tangential B by symmetry.
Determine direction with the right-hand rule before calculating magnitude.
Check near/far limits and continuity at boundaries.

formulas.name: Biot-Savart law
formulas.latex: \mathbf B(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int I\,d\mathbf l'\times\frac{\mathbf r-\mathbf r'}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|^3}
formulas.plain: B = mu0/(4 pi) integral I dl' cross R vector / R^3
conditions: Magnetostatics; replace I dl by J d tau for volume current.
checks: Direction is perpendicular to current element and separation vector.

formulas.name: Ampere's law
formulas.plain: circulation of B = mu0 enclosed steady current; curl B = mu0 J

variables.meaning: signed steady current piercing the loop

conditions: Magnetostatics; use Ampere-Maxwell law when fields vary in time.
checks: The loop orientation and surface normal follow the right-hand rule.

formulas.name: No magnetic monopoles
formulas.plain: div B = 0; net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero
conditions: Classical electromagnetism.
checks: Every field line entering a closed surface also exits.

commonTraps: Using Ampere's law to solve a field without symmetry.
Including currents that do not pierce the chosen surface.
Reversing dl cross R in Biot-Savart.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Magnetic vector potential and magnetic multipoles
recognition: Use A when current geometry or boundary conditions make a curl representation simpler, and use magnetic multipoles far from a localized steady current.
keyIdeas: B = curl A automatically satisfies div B = 0.
A is not unique; gauge changes leave B invariant.
The leading far field of a localized steady current is normally a magnetic dipole.
workflow: Compute A from J or exploit symmetry.
Choose a gauge and differentiate with a curl.
For far fields, compute m and retain the lowest nonzero multipole.
Check div B = 0 and the correct inverse-distance power.

formulas.name: Magnetostatic vector potential
formulas.latex: \mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A,\qquad \mathbf A(\mathbf r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}d\tau'
formulas.plain: B = curl A; A = mu0/(4 pi) integral J/R
conditions: Magnetostatics in Coulomb gauge for the integral form.
checks: A has units tesla meter.

formulas.name: Magnetic dipole moment of a current distribution
formulas.plain: m = one-half integral r' cross J d tau'
conditions: Localized divergence-free current.
checks: For a thin planar loop this reduces to I times oriented area.

formulas.name: Far dipole field
formulas.latex: \mathbf B(\mathbf r)\simeq\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3}[3(\mathbf m\cdot\hat{\mathbf r})\hat{\mathbf r}-\mathbf m]
formulas.plain: B far from magnetic dipole = mu0/(4 pi r^3) times [3(m dot rhat)rhat - m]

variables.meaning: distance much larger than source size

conditions: Outside the localized source; a delta term is needed at the origin for distributional identities.
checks: Field falls as inverse r cubed.

commonTraps: Treating A as unique.
Using the far dipole field inside the source.
Forgetting the factor one-half in the continuous-current moment.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Magnetization, bound currents, H, and magnetic media
recognition: Use M and H to separate material magnetization currents from free currents.
keyIdeas: Magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per volume.
Curl of M acts as a bound volume current and tangential M creates bound surface current.
H tracks free current through its curl, but constitutive behavior can be nonlinear or history dependent.
workflow: Identify free currents and material geometry.
Find M from a constitutive relation or specified dipoles.
Use bound currents with B or free currents with H.
Apply normal B and tangential H boundary conditions.

formulas.name: Bound magnetization currents
formulas.plain: J_bound = curl M; K_bound = M cross outward normal
conditions: Macroscopic magnetization model.
checks: Uniform M has no volume bound current but may have surface current.

formulas.name: Auxiliary H field
formulas.plain: H = B/mu0 - M; curl H = free current density
conditions: Macroscopic magnetostatics.
checks: Tangential H jumps by free surface current.

formulas.name: Linear magnetic medium
formulas.plain: M = chi_m H; B = mu H
conditions: Linear, isotropic, homogeneous medium; not generally valid for ferromagnetic hysteresis.
checks: Vacuum has chi_m = 0 and mu = mu0.

commonTraps: Interchanging free and bound current.
Using B = mu H for a nonlinear magnet without qualification.
Assuming H has zero divergence.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, and motional emf
recognition: Use induction whenever magnetic flux through a circuit changes because the field, loop shape, area, or orientation changes.
keyIdeas: Lenz's law is the sign in Faraday's law and enforces energy conservation.
Transformer emf comes from a nonconservative induced E; motional emf comes from magnetic force on moving charges.
For a moving loop, both effects fit one total-emf expression.
workflow: Choose loop orientation and the corresponding surface normal.
Write the signed flux before differentiating.
Determine whether field change, circuit motion, or both cause the emf.
Use Lenz's law to check the sign physically.

formulas.name: Faraday's law
formulas.latex: \mathcal E=\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l=-d\Phi_B/dt,\qquad \Phi_B=\int\mathbf B\cdot d\mathbf a
formulas.plain: emf = circulation of E = minus time derivative of magnetic flux
conditions: Fixed contour for the simple electric-circulation form.
checks: Induced response opposes the flux change, not necessarily the original flux.

formulas.name: Differential Faraday law
formulas.plain: curl E = -partial B/partial t
conditions: Local Maxwell equation.
checks: Time-varying B makes E nonconservative.

formulas.name: Motional emf
formulas.latex: \mathcal E=\oint(\mathbf E+\mathbf u\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\mathbf l
formulas.plain: emf around moving circuit = integral of E plus circuit velocity cross B dot dl
conditions: Nonrelativistic moving conducting loop.
checks: For a straight rod, polarity follows positive-charge force u cross B.

commonTraps: Differentiating only B while area or orientation also changes.
Using an unsigned flux and then guessing the sign.
Calling induced E conservative.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Inductance, magnetic energy, and RL/LC/RLC transients
recognition: Use an inductor state equation when changing current produces a flux-linked back emf.
keyIdeas: Inductor current cannot jump without an impulse voltage.
An ideal LC circuit exchanges electric and magnetic energy.
RLC behavior is underdamped, critically damped, or overdamped according to the characteristic roots.
workflow: State initial current and capacitor charge.
Write KVL with passive sign conventions.
Find characteristic roots or use the first-order RL form.
Check initial conditions, long-time behavior, and energy loss.

formulas.name: Self and mutual inductance
formulas.plain: flux linkage = L I; self-emf = -L dI/dt; mutual emf = -M dI1/dt
conditions: Linear magnetic response and fixed geometry.
checks: The induced emf opposes the current change.

formulas.name: Magnetic energy
formulas.plain: inductor energy = L I squared/2; vacuum magnetic energy density = B squared/(2 mu0)
conditions: Linear inductor; vacuum field-density form.
checks: Energy is nonnegative and has units joules.

formulas.name: RL step response
formulas.plain: current = final + (initial - final) exp(-t R/L)
conditions: Linear first-order RL circuit.
checks: Current is continuous at switching and reaches If at long time.

formulas.name: Series RLC equation
formulas.plain: L q-double-dot + R q-dot + q/C = applied emf
conditions: Series lumped RLC circuit.
checks: Each term has units volts.

commonTraps: Changing inductor current discontinuously.
Using RC time constant for an RL circuit.
Forgetting mutual-inductance sign depends on winding orientation.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Phasors, impedance, AC power, resonance, and transformers
recognition: Use phasors for linear circuits driven sinusoidally after transients have died away.
keyIdeas: Impedance packages amplitude and phase relations into complex algebra.
Average power is dissipated only by the resistive part of impedance.
Series resonance cancels inductive and capacitive reactance.
workflow: Choose a cosine or sine convention and stay consistent.
Replace elements by impedances and solve the complex circuit.
Convert back to amplitude and phase.
Use rms quantities for average power unless stated otherwise.

formulas.name: Element impedances
formulas.plain: ZR = R; ZL = i omega L; ZC = 1/(i omega C)
conditions: Sinusoidal steady state using exp(i omega t) convention.
checks: Inductor voltage leads current; capacitor voltage lags current.

formulas.name: Series RLC impedance and resonance
formulas.plain: Z = R + i(omega L - 1/(omega C)); resonance omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC)
conditions: Series RLC sinusoidal steady state.
checks: At resonance the reactive part vanishes and current amplitude is maximal for fixed voltage.

formulas.name: Average AC power
formulas.plain: average power = Vrms Irms cos phase = Irms squared R
conditions: Sinusoidal steady state; R is the dissipative series resistance.
checks: Pure L or C has zero average power.

formulas.name: Ideal transformer
formulas.plain: voltage ratio = turns ratio; current ratio is inverse turns ratio
conditions: Ideal transformer with negligible loss and common flux.
checks: Input and output average powers are equal in the ideal limit.

commonTraps: Mixing peak and rms values.
Using DC series-parallel rules without complex phase.
Reversing current and voltage phase for capacitors.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Maxwell equations, displacement current, and charge conservation
recognition: Use the full Maxwell equations when fields vary in time or when consistency with charge conservation matters.
keyIdeas: Displacement current repairs Ampere's law for time-varying electric flux.
Taking the divergence of Ampere-Maxwell yields local charge conservation.
The four equations plus constitutive laws and boundary/initial data determine classical fields.
workflow: Decide whether the problem is electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, or fully dynamical.
Choose integral or differential form from the geometry.
Include both conduction and displacement-current terms.
Check divergence constraints and boundary conditions.

formulas.name: Maxwell equations in vacuum with sources
formulas.latex:
abla\cdot\mathbf E=ho/\epsilon_0,\quad 
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\quad 
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B,\quad 
abla	imes\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E
formulas.plain: div E = rho/epsilon0; div B = 0; curl E = -dB/dt; curl B = mu0 J + mu0 epsilon0 dE/dt
conditions: SI vacuum form; material response may be included in total rho and J or handled with D and H.
checks: Static limits reduce to electrostatics and magnetostatics.

formulas.name: Ampere-Maxwell integral law
formulas.plain: B circulation = mu0 conduction current + mu0 epsilon0 electric-flux rate

variables.meaning: electric flux through the chosen spanning surface

conditions: The same contour can be spanned by any surface when both terms are included.
checks: Units of epsilon0 dPhiE/dt are amperes.

formulas.name: Continuity equation
formulas.plain: charge-density rate + div current density = 0
conditions: Local charge conservation.
checks: A region losing charge has net outward current.

formulas.name: Speed of light
formulas.plain: c = 1/sqrt(mu0 epsilon0)
conditions: Vacuum Maxwell equations.
checks: Dimensions are length per time.

commonTraps: Using magnetostatic Ampere law across a charging capacitor.
Treating displacement current as literal charge transport through vacuum.
Applying only curl equations and ignoring divergence constraints.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Poynting theorem, Maxwell stress, and field momentum
recognition: Use field conservation laws when asked where electromagnetic energy or momentum travels, or when direct force integration is awkward.
keyIdeas: Energy can flow through empty space into a circuit element.
Fields carry momentum density S/c squared.
The Maxwell stress tensor converts field momentum flux into force on enclosed matter.
workflow: Choose a control volume around the system.
Compute energy density and Poynting vector on its boundary.
For force, integrate the stress tensor and include the time derivative of field momentum.
Check global energy or momentum balance.

formulas.name: Vacuum field energy and Poynting vector
formulas.plain: u = one-half(epsilon0 E squared + B squared/mu0); S = E cross B/mu0
conditions: Vacuum fields.
checks: S points in the direction of wave energy propagation.

formulas.name: Poynting theorem
formulas.plain: field-energy rate + div energy flux = minus power delivered to matter

variables.meaning: power per volume delivered to charges

conditions: Local electromagnetic energy conservation.
checks: Positive J dot E decreases field energy unless energy flows in.

formulas.name: Field momentum and stress tensor
formulas.plain: field momentum density g = epsilon0 E cross B = S/c^2; Tij is the Maxwell stress tensor
conditions: Vacuum form.
checks: Integrating stress over a closed surface gives force after accounting for changing field momentum.

commonTraps: Looking only inside a resistor for the source of its delivered energy.
Using S without its direction.
Equating surface stress integral to mechanical force when field momentum is changing and omitting that term.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Vacuum electromagnetic waves, polarization, intensity, and pressure
recognition: Use plane-wave relations in source-free vacuum when fields depend on phase k dot r minus omega t.
keyIdeas: E, B, and the propagation direction are mutually perpendicular for a vacuum plane wave.
The amplitudes obey B0 = E0/c.
Polarization describes the path traced by the electric-field tip at a fixed point.
workflow: Read the phase to identify propagation direction, k, and omega.
Use transversality and the right-hand relation between E and B.
Time-average squared fields for intensity.
Check units and whether peak or rms amplitude is used.

formulas.name: Vacuum wave equation and dispersion
formulas.plain: Laplacian E - mu0 epsilon0 second-time-derivative E = 0; omega = c k
conditions: Source-free vacuum.
checks: Phase and group speeds both equal c.

formulas.name: Plane-wave field relation
formulas.latex: \mathbf B=\frac{1}{c}\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E=\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf B=0
formulas.plain: B = khat cross E / c; both fields are transverse
conditions: Traveling plane wave in vacuum.
checks: E cross B points along khat.

formulas.name: Intensity and radiation pressure
formulas.plain: intensity = one-half c epsilon0 peak-E squared; pressure = I/c for absorption or 2I/c for perfect reflection
conditions: Sinusoidal vacuum wave at normal incidence.
checks: Use twice the pressure only for ideal reflection.

commonTraps: Making E or B longitudinal in a vacuum plane wave.
Using E0 instead of its square in intensity.
Mixing peak and rms amplitudes.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Wave boundary conditions, reflection, and transmission
recognition: Use boundary matching when a plane wave meets an interface between media.
keyIdeas: Tangential E and H are continuous when no free surface charge or current is present.
Frequency is fixed across a stationary boundary, while wavelength changes.
Power coefficients require impedance factors; they are not always the squares of electric-field amplitude coefficients.
workflow: Write incident, reflected, and transmitted phases with a common frequency.
Choose polarization and enforce tangential boundary conditions.
Solve amplitude coefficients.
Convert amplitudes to energy flux and verify R + T = 1 for lossless media.

formulas.name: Normal-incidence amplitude coefficients
formulas.plain: reflected E amplitude ratio = (Z2-Z1)/(Z2+Z1); transmitted ratio = 2 Z2/(Z2+Z1)

variables.meaning: wave impedances of incident and transmitted media

conditions: Normal incidence with the same E-field sign convention on both sides.
checks: If Z1 = Z2, reflection vanishes and tE = 1.

formulas.name: Normal-incidence power coefficients
formulas.plain: reflected power fraction = absolute r squared; transmitted fraction = Z1/Z2 times absolute t squared
conditions: Lossless media with real positive impedances.

formulas.name: Electromagnetic interface conditions
formulas.latex: \hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=0,\quad \hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_f
formulas.plain: tangential E is continuous; tangential H jumps by free surface current
conditions: No singular time-varying magnetic flux sheet; standard macroscopic interface.
checks: Set Kf = 0 for an ordinary dielectric interface.

commonTraps: Squaring tE without the impedance factor to get transmitted power.
Changing frequency at a stationary boundary.
Using normal-component conditions when matching tangential plane-wave fields.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Waves in matter, absorption, dispersion, and conductors
recognition: Use material-wave relations when permittivity, permeability, or conductivity changes propagation speed, attenuation, or phase.
keyIdeas: A complex wave number encodes both phase advance and attenuation.
In a dispersive medium, phase and group velocities differ.
Good conductors exclude high-frequency fields over a skin depth.
workflow: Write the constitutive laws and harmonic time convention.
Derive or use the complex dispersion relation.
Separate the real and imaginary parts of k.
Check vacuum, low-loss, or good-conductor limits.

formulas.name: Wave speed and impedance in a lossless linear medium
formulas.plain: wave speed = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon); impedance = sqrt(mu/epsilon)
conditions: Homogeneous, isotropic, lossless linear medium.
checks: Vacuum gives v = c and Z approximately 377 ohms.

formulas.name: Conducting-medium dispersion
formulas.plain: complex k squared = mu epsilon omega squared + i mu sigma omega
conditions: Harmonic exp[i(kz-omega t)] convention; change of convention conjugates the sign.
checks: Set sigma = 0 to recover the lossless relation.

formulas.name: Good-conductor skin depth
formulas.plain: skin depth = sqrt[2/(mu sigma omega)]
conditions: Good conductor: sigma much greater than omega epsilon.
checks: Higher frequency or conductivity gives shallower penetration.

formulas.name: Phase and group velocity
formulas.plain: phase speed = omega/k; group speed = derivative d omega/dk
conditions: Use real dispersion branches; in lossy media interpret carefully.
checks: For vacuum omega = c k, both equal c.

commonTraps: Treating complex k as an error rather than attenuation.
Equating phase speed with signal speed in a dispersive medium.
Using the good-conductor skin-depth formula outside its limit.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Waveguides and coaxial transmission
recognition: Use guided-wave modes when conducting boundaries confine fields and impose a transverse eigenvalue problem.
keyIdeas: A hollow single-conductor waveguide has cutoff frequencies and no TEM mode.
Above cutoff, longitudinal and transverse wave numbers share the vacuum dispersion budget.
A two-conductor coaxial line can support a TEM mode with no cutoff in the ideal model.
workflow: Choose TE, TM, or TEM mode type from boundary conditions.
Solve the transverse eigenvalue and cutoff wave number.
Find longitudinal propagation constant.
Check whether the drive frequency is above cutoff and verify boundary fields.

formulas.name: Rectangular-waveguide cutoff
formulas.plain: cutoff angular frequency = c pi sqrt[(m/a)^2 + (n/b)^2]
conditions: Ideal perfectly conducting rectangular guide in vacuum; TE and TM index restrictions differ.
checks: Larger guide dimensions lower the cutoff.

formulas.name: Guided dispersion
formulas.plain: longitudinal k squared = omega squared/c squared - cutoff k squared; phase times group speed = c squared
conditions: Lossless hollow guide above cutoff.
checks: Below cutoff kz is imaginary and the mode is evanescent.

formulas.name: Coaxial TEM line parameters
formulas.plain: capacitance per length = 2 pi epsilon/ln(b/a); inductance per length = mu ln(b/a)/(2 pi)
conditions: Ideal concentric coaxial TEM line with homogeneous filling.
checks: Product L'C' = mu epsilon.

commonTraps: Allowing a TEM mode in a hollow one-conductor guide.
Propagating a mode below cutoff as if kz were real.
Confusing guide phase velocity greater than c with information speed.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Scalar/vector potentials, gauges, and retarded sources
recognition: Use time-dependent potentials when sources are known and propagation delay matters, or when gauge choice simplifies Maxwell's equations.
keyIdeas: Potentials have gauge freedom but E and B are gauge invariant.
Lorenz gauge turns the potential equations into sourced wave equations.
Retarded time enforces causal propagation from source to field point.
workflow: Choose scalar and vector potentials and a gauge.
Evaluate sources at retarded time t - R/c.
Differentiate carefully because retarded source values depend on position through R.
Check static and far-field limits.

formulas.name: Fields from time-dependent potentials
formulas.latex: \mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A,\qquad \mathbf E=-\nabla V-\partial\mathbf A/\partial t
formulas.plain: B = curl A; E = -grad V - partial A/partial t
conditions: General classical fields on a simply connected region.
checks: These definitions automatically satisfy div B = 0 and Faraday's law.

formulas.name: Gauge transformation
formulas.plain: A prime = A + grad lambda; V prime = V - partial lambda/partial t
conditions: Gauge-related potentials describe the same fields.
checks: Substitution leaves E and B unchanged.

formulas.name: Lorenz gauge
formulas.plain: div A + mu0 epsilon0 partial V/partial t = 0
conditions: Gauge choice compatible with causal wave equations.
checks: The word is Lorenz, not Lorentz.

formulas.name: Retarded potentials
formulas.latex: V(\mathbf r,t)=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int\frac{\rho(\mathbf r',t-R/c)}{R}d\tau',\quad \mathbf A(\mathbf r,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{\mathbf J(\mathbf r',t-R/c)}{R}d\tau'
formulas.plain: retarded V and A are source integrals evaluated at t - R/c

variables.meaning: source density and current at retarded time

conditions: Lorenz gauge with outgoing causal boundary conditions.
checks: For time-independent sources these reduce to Coulomb and magnetostatic potentials.

commonTraps: Evaluating sources at the observation time instead of retarded time.
Changing A without the corresponding change in V.
Forgetting the partial-A time term in E.

topics.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
topics.title: Lienard-Wiechert potentials and fields of moving charges
familyPatterns: Fields of a Moving Point Charge
recognition: Use Lienard-Wiechert results for a point charge on a specified trajectory when finite propagation time and relativistic beaming matter.
keyIdeas: All source position, velocity, and acceleration quantities are evaluated at the retarded time.
The velocity field falls as inverse distance squared; the acceleration or radiation field falls as inverse distance.
Radiation is transverse in the far zone and is strongest perpendicular to nonrelativistic acceleration.
workflow: Solve the implicit retarded-time equation.
Evaluate R, n, beta, and acceleration at that source event.
Separate near/velocity and far/radiation terms.
Check the static limit and the inverse-distance scaling.

formulas.name: Retarded time for a point charge
formulas.plain: retarded time = observation time - source-to-observer distance at retarded time divided by c
conditions: Causal point-charge trajectory.
checks: The source event lies on the observer's past light cone.

formulas.name: Lienard-Wiechert potentials
formulas.plain: point-charge retarded potentials include the factor (1 - n dot beta) R in the denominator

variables.meaning: unit vector from retarded source position to observer

conditions: Point charge in vacuum.
checks: For v = 0, V becomes the Coulomb potential and A vanishes.

formulas.name: Radiation-zone electric field
formulas.plain: radiation field is proportional to n cross [(n-beta) cross beta-dot] divided by (1-n dot beta)^3 R
conditions: Far-zone inverse-R term for a point charge.
checks: It vanishes for constant velocity and is transverse to n.

commonTraps: Using present-time rather than retarded source data.
Keeping only inverse-square terms when radiation is requested.
Confusing the Lorentz force with the Lorenz gauge.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Energy quantization and thermal radiation
familyPatterns: Quantization of charge, energy, and radiation
recognition: Use this family when the prompt connects temperature to an emission spectrum, asks where a blackbody peaks, or treats energy exchange as integer packets.
keyIdeas: A cavity mode exchanges energy in quanta hf, while a macroscopic blackbody spectrum is obtained by counting modes and weighting their thermal occupation.
Wien's law controls the peak wavelength; Stefan-Boltzmann controls total emitted power. They answer different questions.
Quantized charge and quantized oscillator energy are discrete-counting statements, not claims that position or all energies are always discrete.
workflow: Identify whether the requested quantity is spectral radiance, peak wavelength, total flux, or a number of quanta.
Use absolute temperature and consistent wavelength or frequency units.
Check the hot-object limit: hotter objects peak at shorter wavelength and radiate much more total power.

formulas.name: Photon or oscillator quantum
formulas.plain: E_n = n h f = n hbar omega
conditions: Use for quantized mode energy; a harmonic oscillator also carries a zero-point term treated in its own topic.
checks: Energy spacing is hf.
n is dimensionless and discrete.

formulas.name: Planck spectral radiance
formulas.plain: B_lambda = (2 h c^2/lambda^5)/(exp[h c/(lambda k_B T)] - 1)
conditions: Ideal blackbody in thermal equilibrium; do not mix B_lambda with a frequency-density form.
checks: The exponential argument is dimensionless.
Long wavelengths recover the Rayleigh-Jeans trend.

formulas.name: Wien displacement law
formulas.plain: lambda_max T = b

variables.meaning: Wien displacement constant, about 2.898e-3 m K

conditions: Peak of the wavelength spectrum B_lambda, not the peak of B_frequency.
checks: Doubling T halves lambda_max.

formulas.name: Stefan-Boltzmann emission
formulas.plain: P = emissivity sigma A T^4
conditions: Total emitted power; for net radiative exchange use epsilon sigma A (T^4 - T_env^4).
checks: Power scales as area and the fourth power of absolute temperature.

commonTraps: Using Celsius in a thermal-radiation law.
Treating the wavelength and frequency versions of Planck's spectrum as if their maxima convert by f=c/lambda.
Using Wien's law when the question asks total power.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Photons, photoelectric emission, Compton scattering, and X-rays
familyPatterns: 3-4 X Rays and the Compton Effect
X-rays, Compton scattering, and photon momentum
recognition: Use photon bookkeeping when light exchanges energy or momentum in individual events: electron emission, photon-electron collisions, or characteristic and cutoff X-rays.
keyIdeas: Photon energy is set by frequency; photon momentum is set by wavelength.
Photoelectric intensity primarily controls event rate, while frequency controls the maximum kinetic energy.
Compton scattering requires relativistic energy-momentum conservation for the electron-photon system.
workflow: Draw the before-and-after particles and assign energy and momentum to each.
For photoemission, subtract the material work function before converting kinetic energy to speed or stopping potential.
For X-ray tubes, distinguish the bremsstrahlung cutoff from discrete characteristic lines.

formulas.name: Photon energy and momentum
formulas.plain: E_gamma = h f = h c/lambda; p_gamma = E_gamma/c = h/lambda
conditions: Photon in vacuum; use medium wave relations only when the problem explicitly models them.
checks: E = pc for a photon.
Shorter wavelength means larger energy and momentum.

formulas.name: Photoelectric equation
formulas.plain: K_max = h f - work function = e times stopping potential
conditions: Single-photon photoemission with incident frequency above threshold f_0=phi/h.
checks: At threshold K_max is zero.
Increasing intensity at fixed frequency does not raise K_max in this model.

formulas.name: Compton wavelength shift
formulas.plain: lambda_final - lambda_initial = h/(m_e c) times (1 - cos theta)
conditions: Scattering from an initially free electron at rest.
checks: No shift at zero angle.
Maximum shift is 2h/(m_e c) at 180 degrees.

formulas.name: X-ray tube cutoff
formulas.plain: e V = h f_max = h c/lambda_min
conditions: Ideal upper bound when one electron gives all its kinetic energy to one photon.
checks: Larger voltage produces a shorter cutoff wavelength.

commonTraps: Using classical intensity to predict a higher photoelectron endpoint energy.
Applying nonrelativistic photon momentum.
Confusing a characteristic X-ray line with the tube cutoff.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Rutherford scattering, Bohr atoms, and discrete spectra
familyPatterns: Atomic spectra, Rutherford scattering, and the Bohr model
recognition: Use these semiclassical models for nuclear size or Coulomb-scattering estimates, hydrogenic radii and energies, line spectra, and excitation thresholds.
keyIdeas: Rutherford scattering follows from a repulsive inverse-square Coulomb interaction and exposes a compact positive nucleus.
The Bohr model correctly captures hydrogenic energy scaling even though full quantum mechanics replaces its literal circular orbits.
Spectral photons carry differences between stationary-state energies, not the absolute binding energy unless one state is the continuum.
workflow: Identify nuclear charge Z, projectile charge z, and whether the event is head-on or at a scattering angle.
For a hydrogenic ion, write E_n first and take a final-minus-initial difference with signs visible.
Check emission versus absorption: emission lowers the atomic energy and produces a positive photon energy.

formulas.name: Head-on Coulomb closest approach
formulas.plain: initial kinetic energy = k_e Z z e^2/r_min
conditions: Repulsive head-on encounter, heavy fixed nucleus, nonrelativistic energy conservation.
checks: Higher kinetic energy gives a smaller closest approach.

formulas.name: Rutherford differential cross section
formulas.plain: d sigma/d Omega = [Z z e^2/(16 pi epsilon_0 K)]^2 csc^4(theta/2)

variables.meaning: projectile kinetic energy far from the target

conditions: Point Coulomb charges, single scattering, target recoil neglected.
checks: Units are area per solid angle.
Large-angle events are rare.

formulas.name: Hydrogenic Bohr radius and energy
conditions: One-electron atom or ion with a heavy nucleus; use reduced mass for precision.
checks: Binding weakens as n grows.
Ionization corresponds to E=0.

formulas.name: Spectral transition
formulas.plain: h f = absolute energy difference; 1/lambda = R Z^2 times absolute inverse-square difference

variables.meaning: Rydberg constant for an infinitely heavy nucleus

conditions: Hydrogenic transition; correct the Rydberg constant for reduced mass when needed.
checks: Photon energy is positive.
Emission has n_i greater than n_f in the Bohr model.

formulas.name: Franck-Hertz excitation spacing
formulas.plain: electron charge times voltage spacing = excitation-energy spacing
conditions: Electrons gain energy through a potential difference and lose a fixed excitation quantum in inelastic collisions.
checks: One electron-volt corresponds to one volt times the elementary charge.

commonTraps: Forgetting that bound-state energies are negative.
Subtracting levels in the wrong order and carrying a negative photon energy.
Treating the Bohr orbit as the modern spatial probability distribution.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Matter waves, diffraction, and wave packets
familyPatterns: de Broglie wavelength and particle diffraction
Wave packets, phase velocity, and group velocity
Wave-particle duality, interference, and which-path information
recognition: Use matter-wave relations when a particle beam diffracts or interferes, when a localized packet is built from many wave numbers, or when phase and envelope motion must be separated.
keyIdeas: The de Broglie relation connects mechanical momentum to spatial phase.
Localization requires a spread in wave number; the envelope travels at group velocity.
Which-path information destroys the coherence needed for a stable interference pattern even if individual detections remain localized.
workflow: Find the particle momentum using the correct relativistic or nonrelativistic relation.
Convert momentum to wavelength, then apply the diffraction geometry.
For a packet, use the dispersion relation omega(k) before calculating phase or group velocity.

formulas.name: de Broglie relation
formulas.plain: lambda = h/p; wave number k = p/hbar
conditions: Applies to free-particle momentum eigenstates; calculate p from the applicable energy relation.
checks: Larger momentum means shorter wavelength.

formulas.name: Nonrelativistic accelerated particle
formulas.plain: p = sqrt(2 m K) = sqrt(2 m absolute-charge V)
conditions: Starts from rest and K is much smaller than mc squared.
checks: Use a relativistic momentum when the voltage is not small compared with mc squared per charge.

formulas.name: Bragg diffraction
formulas.plain: 2 d sin theta = n lambda
conditions: Constructive reflection from parallel lattice planes; angle convention must match the geometry.
checks: The right side cannot exceed 2d for a physical sine.

formulas.name: Phase and group velocities
formulas.plain: phase speed = omega/k; group speed = derivative of omega with respect to k
conditions: A narrow packet in k-space; for a nonrelativistic free particle v_g=p/m.
checks: The packet velocity should match the classical particle velocity in the free nonrelativistic limit.

commonTraps: Using p=mv at relativistic speeds.
Confusing the motion of a phase crest with the motion of the packet.
Assuming interference survives after the alternatives become distinguishable.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Probability density, normalization, and probability current
familyPatterns: Probability density, normalization, probability current, and boundary behavior
Probability in the middle third of a box
recognition: Start here whenever the question asks whether a wavefunction is physical, requests a probability in a region, or tracks probability flow across a boundary.
keyIdeas: The wavefunction is a probability amplitude; measurable position probability comes from its modulus squared.
Normalization fixes an overall magnitude but not a global phase.
Probability conservation is local: changes in density are balanced by the divergence of current.
workflow: Check square integrability and boundary behavior before normalizing.
Integrate the density only over the requested region and divide by the total norm if the state was not normalized.
For flow, compute the phase-sensitive current rather than inferring motion from the density alone.

formulas.name: Normalization and regional probability
formulas.plain: integral of absolute psi squared over all space = 1; probability in R = integral over R
conditions: Pure state represented in position space.
checks: Probabilities are between zero and one.
The density has inverse-volume units in three dimensions.

formulas.name: Expectation and variance of position
formulas.plain: mean x = integral psi-star x psi; variance = mean x-squared minus mean-x squared
conditions: Normalized state with finite moments.
checks: Variance cannot be negative.
Symmetry can force the mean to zero without forcing the variance to zero.

formulas.name: Probability current
formulas.plain: j = hbar/(2 m i) times (psi-star grad psi minus psi grad psi-star)
conditions: Single nonrelativistic particle with the standard kinetic term and no vector potential.
checks: A real stationary spatial wavefunction has zero current.
A plane wave has current parallel to momentum.

formulas.name: Continuity equation
formulas.plain: time derivative of density plus divergence of current = 0
conditions: Hermitian Hamiltonian with probability-conserving boundary conditions.
checks: Integrating over all space gives constant total probability if boundary flux vanishes.

commonTraps: Integrating psi instead of absolute psi squared.
Dropping a Jacobian such as r squared sin theta in curvilinear coordinates.
Interpreting a stationary density as proof that the state has zero momentum.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Schrodinger dynamics and stationary states
familyPatterns: 6-1 The Schrodinger Equation in One Dimension
Stationary states and the time-independent Schrodinger equation
Time-dependent Schrodinger equation and time evolution
recognition: Use this framework when a state evolves in time, when boundary conditions select energy eigenstates, or when an initial state must be expanded in stationary states.
keyIdeas: The Hamiltonian generates time evolution; its eigenvalue problem supplies stationary-state building blocks.
A single energy eigenstate changes only by a phase, so its probability density is time independent.
A superposition evolves through relative phases, which can make observables oscillate.
workflow: Write the Hamiltonian with the correct coordinates, potential, and domain.
Solve the time-independent eigenvalue problem with boundary and matching conditions.
Project the initial state onto the eigenbasis, attach each phase exp(-i E_n t/hbar), and recombine.

formulas.name: Time-dependent Schrodinger equation
formulas.plain: i hbar time-derivative of state = Hamiltonian acting on state
conditions: Nonrelativistic quantum dynamics; H may be time dependent.
checks: A Hermitian H preserves norm.
Both sides have energy times state units.

formulas.name: Time-independent Schrodinger equation
formulas.plain: Hamiltonian phi_n = E_n phi_n
conditions: Time-independent Hamiltonian and stationary-state separation.
checks: Boundary conditions determine the allowed eigenvalues.

formulas.name: Eigenstate expansion and evolution
formulas.plain: psi(t) = sum c_n phase_n times energy eigenstate n; c_n is projection of initial state
conditions: Complete orthonormal discrete energy basis; replace the sum or add an integral for a continuum.
checks: The probabilities |c_n| squared are constant for a time-independent H.
Relative phases carry observable time dependence.

formulas.name: Time-evolution operator
formulas.plain: U(t) = exponential of -i H t/hbar
conditions: Time-independent Hamiltonian; use a time-ordered exponential otherwise.
checks: U dagger U = identity.
At t=0, U is identity.

commonTraps: Solving an eigenvalue equation without enforcing the physical domain and boundary conditions.
Giving every component the same time phase in a superposition.
Confusing a stationary state with a particle literally at rest.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Observables, operators, Hilbert space, and measurement
familyPatterns: Expectation values, moments, variance, and Ehrenfest behavior
Hilbert space, Dirac notation, bases, and representation changes
Measurement, collapse, pure states, and mixed states
Observables, Hermitian operators, eigenvalues, and eigenfunction expansions
recognition: Use operator language when asked for possible measurement outcomes, probabilities in a basis, expectation values, compatibility, or a representation change.
keyIdeas: An observable is represented by a Hermitian operator; its eigenvalues are possible ideal measurement results.
Amplitudes are inner products. Their squared magnitudes give probabilities after the relevant basis is normalized.
A basis change alters coordinates, not the physical state or basis-independent predictions.
workflow: Identify the operator and its spectrum, including any degeneracy or continuum normalization.
Expand the state in the operator eigenbasis.
Compute probabilities or moments, then verify normalization and reality of observable expectations.

formulas.name: Position and momentum operators
formulas.plain: x operator multiplies by x; p_x operator = -i hbar derivative with respect to x
conditions: Position representation with a domain and boundary conditions that make momentum self-adjoint.
checks: Applying p_x to exp(i k x) yields hbar k times the same function.

formulas.name: Expectation value
formulas.plain: mean A = bra psi times operator A times ket psi
conditions: Normalized state in the domain of A.
checks: The expectation of a Hermitian observable is real.

formulas.name: Measurement probabilities
formulas.plain: probability of eigenvalue a_n = absolute projection amplitude squared
conditions: For degeneracy, sum squared projections onto the full eigenspace; use densities for a continuum.
checks: Probabilities over a complete basis sum to one.

formulas.name: Completeness
formulas.plain: sum of projectors over a complete orthonormal basis = identity
conditions: Discrete complete orthonormal basis; continuous labels require integrals and delta normalization.
checks: Inserting completeness must leave any state unchanged.

formulas.name: Ehrenfest relations
formulas.plain: d mean-x/dt = mean-p/m; d mean-p/dt = minus mean potential slope
conditions: Hamiltonian p squared/(2m) + V(x) with suitable boundary behavior.
checks: The second relation has the form mean force.

commonTraps: Squaring an amplitude before taking its absolute value.
Treating an expectation value as the only possible outcome.
Ignoring degeneracy when projecting onto a measured eigenvalue.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Commutators, compatible observables, and uncertainty
familyPatterns: 5-6 Some Consequences of the Uncertainty Principle
Commutators, compatible observables, and simultaneous eigenstates
recognition: Use commutators to test simultaneous sharpness or conserved quantities, and use uncertainty inequalities to bound spreads rather than measurement error.
keyIdeas: Noncommuting observables need not possess simultaneous eigenstates and cannot both have arbitrarily small standard deviations in one state.
The lower bound is state dependent through the commutator expectation.
Energy-time uncertainty is not usually an operator-pair relation because time is a parameter in ordinary quantum mechanics.
workflow: Compute the commutator before selecting an uncertainty formula.
Calculate variances from second moments, not from mean absolute deviations.
Check whether equality is actually justified; most states do not saturate the bound.

formulas.name: Commutator
formulas.latex: [\hat A,\hat B]=\hat A\hat B-\hat B\hat A
formulas.plain: [A,B] = AB - BA
conditions: Operators share a suitable common domain.

formulas.name: Canonical commutator
formulas.plain: [x,p_x] = i hbar
conditions: Canonical position and momentum on their physical domain.
checks: The commutator has action units.

formulas.name: Robertson uncertainty relation
formulas.plain: sigma_A sigma_B is at least one half the absolute mean commutator
conditions: Normalized state in the required operator domains; the stronger Schrodinger relation also includes covariance.
checks: For x and p, the bound is hbar/2.

formulas.name: Energy-time scale
formulas.plain: energy spread times characteristic evolution or lifetime is of order at least hbar/2

variables.meaning: process lifetime or characteristic change time, defined by context

conditions: Use only after defining the physical time scale; it is not a universal measurement-operator statement.
checks: Short-lived states have broad energy lines.

commonTraps: Calling uncertainty an instrument defect.
Concluding that commuting operators always have nondegenerate shared eigenvectors.
Replacing an inequality by equality without showing a minimum-uncertainty state.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Free particles, momentum space, and Fourier transforms
familyPatterns: 10.1 The Free Particle in Cartesian Coordinates
10.2 The Free Particle in Spherical Coordinates
Free particles, momentum representation, and Fourier transforms
recognition: Use this topic when V is constant or zero, momentum is sharp or distributed, or a localized packet must be transformed between position and momentum space.
keyIdeas: A single plane wave is a momentum eigenstate but is not square normalizable on infinite space.
Localized states are superpositions of plane waves; position width and momentum width are Fourier-linked.
Box normalization and Dirac-delta normalization are conventions that must not be mixed mid-calculation.
workflow: Choose continuum delta normalization or a finite normalization box and state the choice.
Obtain the dispersion E(p), evolve each momentum amplitude by its phase, then inverse transform.
Use flux, not just amplitude squared, when comparing traveling-wave channels with different wave numbers.

formulas.name: Free-particle dispersion
formulas.plain: E = p squared/(2m) = hbar squared k squared/(2m); plane wave phase is k dot r minus omega t
conditions: Nonrelativistic free particle.
checks: Momentum is hbar k.
Group velocity is hbar k/m.

formulas.name: Position-momentum transform
formulas.plain: phi(p) = 1/sqrt(2 pi hbar) integral exp(-i p x/hbar) psi(x) dx
conditions: One-dimensional symmetric Fourier convention; use the matching inverse transform.
checks: Integral of |phi| squared over p equals one when psi is normalized.

formulas.name: Continuum orthogonality
formulas.plain: momentum eigenkets have delta normalization and integrate to identity
conditions: Continuum-normalized momentum eigenstates.
checks: Individual plane waves are generalized states, not unit-normalized square-integrable functions.

commonTraps: Normalizing a plane wave to one over all infinite space.
Dropping the hbar in a p-space Fourier phase.
Comparing transmission amplitudes without the corresponding velocity or wave-number factor.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Infinite square well and superposition dynamics
familyPatterns: 7.4 The Quantum Particle in a Box
Infinite square well and superposition dynamics
recognition: Use the box model when a particle is confined by impenetrable endpoints, giving sinusoidal eigenstates, n-squared energies, and clean superposition dynamics.
keyIdeas: The wavefunction vanishes at infinite-potential walls, quantizing the allowed wave number.
Different energy components acquire different phases, creating time-dependent interference in density and observables.
Parity and orthogonality often eliminate integrals before calculation.
workflow: Declare the interval; formulas for 0 to L differ in appearance from those for a centered well.
Expand the initial state in normalized sine or parity eigenfunctions.
Use orthogonality for normalization and moments, and retain cross terms when the observable can connect components.

formulas.name: Box eigenstates on 0 to L
formulas.plain: phi_n = sqrt(2/L) sin(n pi x/L)
conditions: Infinite walls at x=0 and x=L.
checks: State vanishes at both endpoints.
Each state integrates to unit probability.

formulas.name: Box energies
formulas.plain: E_n = n squared pi squared hbar squared/(2 m L squared)
conditions: One-dimensional infinite square well.
checks: Ground energy is nonzero.
Energy scales as 1/L squared.

formulas.name: Expansion coefficient
formulas.plain: c_n = overlap integral of eigenstate n with initial wavefunction
conditions: Normalized eigenbasis on the stated interval.
checks: Sum of |c_n| squared is one for a normalized initial state.

formulas.name: Revival time
formulas.plain: revival time = 4 m L squared/(pi hbar)

variables.meaning: full phase-revival time for the standard box spectrum

conditions: Infinite well with E_n proportional to n squared; shorter fractional or observable periods may occur.
checks: Has units of time and scales as L squared.

commonTraps: Using n=0 as a box eigenstate.
Forgetting that the chosen coordinate interval changes parity and sine/cosine forms.
Dropping superposition cross terms when calculating a noncommuting observable.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Finite wells, delta potentials, tunneling, and scattering
familyPatterns: Finite wells, delta potentials, tunneling, and reflection or transmission
recognition: Use piecewise stationary states when the potential changes by region, with oscillatory solutions where E exceeds V and exponential solutions where E is below V.
keyIdeas: Finite discontinuities preserve psi and its first derivative; a delta potential creates a known derivative jump.
Bound states decay outside the well and are selected by matching conditions.
Transmission and reflection are flux ratios. Nonzero tunneling does not mean energy conservation is violated.
workflow: Draw V(x), mark each region, and define each real wave number or decay constant.
Keep only physically allowed exponentials at infinity.
Apply continuity and derivative rules, solve the resulting linear or transcendental equations, then form flux ratios.

formulas.name: Regional wave and decay numbers
formulas.plain: k = sqrt(2m(E-V))/hbar; kappa = sqrt(2m(V-E))/hbar
conditions: Piecewise constant nonrelativistic potential.
checks: Both k and kappa have inverse-length units.

formulas.name: Finite symmetric-well conditions
formulas.plain: k tan(k a) = kappa for even states; -k cot(k a) = kappa for odd states
conditions: Well V=-V0 for |x|<a and V=0 outside, with -V0<E<0.
checks: Solutions alternate parity.
Deeper or wider wells support more roots.

formulas.name: Delta-potential derivative jump
formulas.plain: derivative jump = 2 m alpha/hbar squared times psi at the delta
conditions: One-dimensional delta potential; psi itself remains continuous.
checks: Attractive alpha is negative in this sign convention.

formulas.name: Attractive delta bound energy
formulas.plain: E = -m alpha squared/(2 hbar squared) for an attractive delta

variables.meaning: positive attractive strength in V=-alpha delta

conditions: Single attractive delta on the full line; exactly one bound state.
checks: Energy is negative and depends on alpha squared.

formulas.name: WKB tunneling estimate
formulas.plain: T approximately exp[-2 integral through forbidden region of sqrt(2m(V-E))/hbar dx]
conditions: Slowly varying barrier and a sufficiently opaque forbidden region; prefactors may matter for precision.
checks: The exponent is dimensionless.
Thicker or taller barriers reduce T exponentially.

formulas.name: Flux conservation
formulas.plain: reflection plus transmission = 1; transmission is transmitted flux divided by incident flux
conditions: Real time-independent potential with one incident channel and no absorption.
checks: R and T lie between zero and one.

commonTraps: Forcing the derivative to be continuous across a delta potential.
Keeping an exponential that diverges at spatial infinity.
Calling an amplitude ratio a probability without converting it to a flux ratio.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Quantum harmonic oscillator
familyPatterns: Quantum harmonic oscillator: analytic and ladder-operator methods
recognition: Use the oscillator for a quadratic potential or for small motion near any stable equilibrium, especially when ladder operators can replace differential equations.
keyIdeas: The energy levels are equally spaced and include irreducible zero-point energy.
Ladder operators change n by one with normalization factors fixed by the number operator.
Position and momentum connect only neighboring number states, producing simple selection rules.
workflow: Identify omega from V approximately one half m omega squared x squared.
Choose the analytic wavefunction or ladder-operator route based on the requested quantity.
Use orthogonality and ladder action before integrating.

formulas.name: Oscillator spectrum
formulas.plain: E_n = hbar omega (n + 1/2)
conditions: One-dimensional ideal harmonic oscillator.
checks: Adjacent levels differ by hbar omega.
Ground energy is hbar omega/2.

formulas.name: Ladder definitions
formulas.plain: a = sqrt(m omega/(2 hbar)) times (x + i p/(m omega)); [a,a dagger]=1
conditions: Canonical x and p oscillator algebra.
checks: The operator inside each definition is dimensionless overall.

formulas.name: Ladder action
formulas.plain: a lowers n with sqrt(n); a dagger raises n with sqrt(n+1)
conditions: Normalized oscillator number states.
checks: a annihilates the ground state.

formulas.name: Position and momentum in ladder form
formulas.plain: x = sqrt(hbar/(2m omega))(a+a dagger); p = -i sqrt(m hbar omega/2)(a-a dagger)
conditions: Harmonic oscillator basis.
checks: x connects n only to n plus or minus one.

formulas.name: Ground-state width
formulas.plain: sigma_x = sqrt(hbar/(2m omega)); sigma_p = sqrt(m hbar omega/2)
conditions: Oscillator ground state.
checks: Their product is hbar/2.

commonTraps: Dropping the one-half zero-point contribution.
Applying a lowering operator to the ground state as if it produced n=-1.
Losing square-root normalization factors in repeated ladder operations.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Three-dimensional Schrodinger equation and spherical separation
familyPatterns: 7-1 The Schrodinger Equation in Three Dimensions
Three-dimensional Schrodinger equation and spherical separation
recognition: Use spherical separation for central potentials, where angular momentum labels the angular functions and the radial equation contains an effective centrifugal term.
keyIdeas: A central potential commutes with L squared and L_z, so states can be labeled by l and m.
Writing u(r)=rR(r) turns the radial problem into a one-dimensional-looking equation on r greater than or equal to zero.
The measure matters: radial probability uses r squared |R| squared dr, or equivalently |u| squared dr.
workflow: Test whether the potential depends only on r.
Separate psi into R(r) Y_l^m(theta,phi), enforce angular single-valuedness, and solve the radial equation.
Apply regularity at the origin, decay or scattering conditions at infinity, and normalize with the spherical measure.

formulas.name: Three-dimensional Hamiltonian
formulas.plain: H = -hbar squared/(2m) Laplacian + V(r)
conditions: Single nonrelativistic spinless particle without electromagnetic vector potential.
checks: Kinetic and potential terms both have energy units.

formulas.name: Spherical Laplacian
formulas.plain: Laplacian = radial derivative term minus L squared/(hbar squared r squared)
conditions: Spherical coordinates acting on scalar wavefunctions.
checks: The angular term scales as inverse r squared.

formulas.name: Reduced radial equation
formulas.plain: -hbar squared/(2m) u-double-prime + [V + hbar squared l(l+1)/(2m r squared)]u = E u
conditions: Central potential after separation.
checks: u(0)=0 for regular physical solutions.
The centrifugal term vanishes for l=0.

formulas.name: Spherical normalization
formulas.plain: integral |R| squared r squared dr = integral |u| squared dr = 1
conditions: Normalized angular spherical harmonic.
checks: Do not include an extra r squared when using u.

commonTraps: Normalizing R with dr instead of r squared dr.
Forgetting the centrifugal term.
Allowing a reduced radial solution that makes the full wavefunction singular or nonnormalizable at the origin.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Orbital angular momentum and spherical harmonics
familyPatterns: 9.2 Eigenvalues of the Angular Momentum Operators
9.3 Eigenfunctions of the Orbital Angular Momentum Operators
Orbital angular momentum algebra and spherical harmonics
recognition: Use angular-momentum algebra when rotational symmetry, L squared and a component, spherical harmonics, or angular ladder operations appear.
keyIdeas: Only one Cartesian component can be sharp along with total angular momentum.
The quantum numbers satisfy l=0,1,2,... and m=-l,...,l.
Ladder operators determine spectra and matrix elements without directly solving angular differential equations.
workflow: Choose a quantization axis and label the state |l,m>.
Use commutators and ladder actions before writing differential operators.
Translate to spherical harmonics only when an angular probability or coordinate-space integral is needed.

formulas.name: Orbital angular momentum
formulas.plain: L = r cross p
conditions: Orbital motion relative to the chosen origin.
checks: L has action units and is perpendicular to r and p classically.

formulas.name: Angular-momentum algebra
formulas.plain: [L_i,L_j] = i hbar epsilon_ijk L_k; L squared commutes with every component
conditions: Any angular-momentum operator obeying the rotation algebra.
checks: Cyclic component order gives a positive sign.

formulas.name: Angular-momentum eigenvalues
formulas.plain: L squared eigenvalue = hbar squared l(l+1); L_z eigenvalue = hbar m
conditions: Orbital angular momentum has integer l.
checks: There are 2l+1 m values for each l.

formulas.name: Angular ladder action
formulas.plain: L plus/minus changes m by plus/minus one with the standard square-root factor

variables.meaning: L_x plus or minus i L_y

conditions: Normalized |l,m> states.
checks: Raising annihilates m=l; lowering annihilates m=-l.

formulas.name: Spherical-harmonic orthonormality
formulas.plain: integral over solid angle of Y_lm-star Y_l-prime-m-prime = two Kronecker deltas

variables.meaning: sin theta d theta d phi

conditions: Standard normalized spherical harmonics.
checks: The integral of |Y_lm| squared is one.

commonTraps: Using l squared hbar squared instead of l(l+1) hbar squared.
Allowing |m| greater than l.
Assuming two different Cartesian components can both be sharp in a nonzero-angular-momentum state.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Hydrogenic atoms: spectrum, wavefunctions, and probabilities
familyPatterns: 7-2 Quantization of Angular Momentum and Energy in the Hydrogen Atom
Hydrogen atom: radial wavefunctions, spectrum, degeneracy, and probabilities
recognition: Use the Coulomb central-potential solution for one-electron atoms and ions, including quantum numbers, degeneracy, radial probability, and transition energies.
keyIdeas: The nonrelativistic Coulomb energy depends only on n, creating degeneracy in l and m before fine structure or external fields.
The wavefunction separates into radial and angular factors; the most probable radius is not generally the expectation radius.
Nodes and near-origin behavior follow from n and l and are powerful qualitative checks.
workflow: Identify Z and use the electron-nucleus reduced mass if precision matters.
List allowed n, l, and m values before counting states or evaluating operators.
Use radial probability 4 pi r squared |psi| squared for s states, or r squared |R_nl| squared after angular integration.

formulas.name: Hydrogenic Hamiltonian
formulas.plain: H = -hbar squared/(2 reduced mass) Laplacian - k_e Z e squared/r
conditions: Nonrelativistic one-electron ion without spin-dependent corrections.
checks: Potential is attractive and approaches zero from below.

formulas.name: Hydrogenic energy
formulas.plain: E_n = - reduced-mass times Z squared e fourth divided by 2(4 pi epsilon_0) squared hbar squared n squared
conditions: Coulomb spectrum before fine structure and external fields.
checks: Scales as -Z squared/n squared.
Approaches zero from below as n grows.

formulas.name: Quantum-number ranges
formulas.plain: n positive; l from zero through n minus one; m from minus l through l

variables.meaning: principal, orbital, and magnetic quantum numbers

conditions: Hydrogenic spatial states.
checks: Ignoring spin, each n shell contains n squared spatial states.

formulas.name: Separated wavefunction and radial probability
formulas.plain: psi_nlm = radial function times spherical harmonic; radial probability = r squared |R| squared dr
conditions: Normalized angular functions.
checks: Angular probability integrates out of the radial distribution.

formulas.name: Hydrogenic length scale
formulas.plain: hydrogenic radius scale = 4 pi epsilon_0 hbar squared/(reduced mass Z e squared), approximately a_0/Z
conditions: Hydrogenic ion; approximation uses electron mass in a_0.
checks: Larger Z contracts the wavefunction.

commonTraps: Counting only one l value per shell.
Using |R| squared rather than r squared |R| squared for a radial probability plot.
Claiming every state with the same n remains degenerate after perturbations are introduced.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Spin one-half, Pauli matrices, and Stern-Gerlach measurements
familyPatterns: Spin one-half, Pauli matrices, and Stern-Gerlach measurements
recognition: Use two-component spinors and Pauli matrices when a spin-one-half particle is prepared or measured along different axes.
keyIdeas: Spin is intrinsic angular momentum, not a literal rotating classical sphere.
A state sharp along one axis is generally a superposition of up and down along another.
The Bloch-vector direction determines measurement probabilities for any analyzer axis.
workflow: Choose and state a basis, usually the S_z eigenbasis.
Write the normalized spinor and the operator for the requested direction.
Project onto the analyzer eigenvectors or use the Bloch-vector dot product.

formulas.name: Pauli matrices and spin
formulas.plain: sigma_x, sigma_y, sigma_z are the standard Pauli matrices; S = hbar/2 times sigma
conditions: Spin-one-half Hilbert space in the S_z basis.
checks: Each Pauli matrix squares to identity.
Spin-component eigenvalues are plus or minus hbar/2.

formulas.name: Pauli algebra
formulas.plain: sigma_i sigma_j = delta_ij identity + i epsilon_ijk sigma_k
conditions: Standard Pauli matrices.
checks: The anticommutator is 2 delta_ij I.

formulas.name: General pure spinor
formulas.plain: spin up along n = cos(theta/2) up-z + exp(i phi) sin(theta/2) down-z

variables.meaning: polar and azimuthal angles of the Bloch vector

conditions: Normalized pure spin-one-half state, up to a global phase.
checks: Probabilities in the z basis sum to one.

formulas.name: Spin analyzer probability
formulas.plain: probability of up along m given up along n = (1+m dot n)/2 = cos squared(gamma/2)

variables.meaning: angle between preparation and analyzer axes

conditions: Pure spin-up preparation and ideal projective measurement.
checks: Same axis gives one; opposite axis gives zero; perpendicular axes give one half.

commonTraps: Using theta instead of theta/2 in a spinor.
Changing basis without transforming both state and operator consistently.
Treating a global phase as observable.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Angular-momentum addition, magnetic moments, and Zeeman dynamics
familyPatterns: 8.2 Orbital Magnetic Dipole Moment of the Electron
9.5 Total Angular Momentum for Two or More Electrons
11.8 The Magnetic Moment of an Electron
11.9 Precession of an Electron in a Magnetic Field
Magnetic moments, spin-orbit ideas, and the Zeeman effect
recognition: Use coupled angular-momentum algebra when two angular momenta combine, or when magnetic fields and spin-orbit interactions split or precess states.
keyIdeas: The allowed total j values run from |j1-j2| through j1+j2 in unit steps.
Coupled and uncoupled bases are two complete descriptions connected by Clebsch-Gordan coefficients.
Magnetic interactions are dot products; the sign and g factor determine energy ordering and precession.
workflow: List allowed total quantum numbers and compare the coupled versus uncoupled basis dimensions.
Use J squared identities to evaluate dot products such as L dot S.
Write H prime = -mu dot B and only then substitute charge signs and g factors.

formulas.name: Addition rule
formulas.plain: J = J1 + J2; total j runs from absolute difference to sum

variables.meaning: component and total angular-momentum quantum numbers

conditions: Addition of two angular momenta.
checks: Sum over coupled multiplet dimensions equals (2j1+1)(2j2+1).

formulas.name: Angular-momentum dot product
formulas.plain: J1 dot J2 = one half (J squared - J1 squared - J2 squared)
conditions: Operators for distinct subsystems commute.
checks: Useful in a coupled basis because every squared operator is diagonal.

formulas.name: Electron magnetic moments
formulas.plain: mu_L = -mu_B L/hbar; mu_S = -g_s mu_B S/hbar
conditions: Electron orbital and spin magnetic moments; signs reflect negative electron charge.
checks: Magnetic moment is antiparallel to electron angular momentum.

formulas.name: Zeeman interaction
formulas.plain: Zeeman Hamiltonian = minus magnetic moment dot magnetic field
conditions: Magnetic dipole in an applied field; weak- or strong-field basis must match other couplings.
checks: Energy is lowest when the magnetic moment aligns with B.

formulas.name: Larmor precession scale
formulas.plain: precession angular frequency = absolute g times magneton times B/hbar
conditions: Isolated angular momentum with a linear Zeeman Hamiltonian; sign sets precession sense.
checks: Frequency is proportional to field strength.

commonTraps: Adding quantum numbers as if only j=j1+j2 were allowed.
Forgetting the electron's negative charge in its magnetic moment.
Using an uncoupled basis after spin-orbit coupling has made total J the natural good quantum number.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Two-particle systems, exchange symmetry, atoms, and molecules
familyPatterns: 12.6 Application of Symmetrization Rules to the Helium Atom
7-6 The Schrodinger Equation for Two or More Particles
7-7 Ground States of Atoms: The Periodic Table
8.4 The Exclusion Principle and the Periodic Table
Exclusion principle, multielectron atoms, periodic structure, spectra, and lasers
recognition: Use exchange symmetry when particles are identical, and separate center-of-mass from relative motion when a two-body interaction depends only on separation.
keyIdeas: Identical boson states are symmetric under exchange; identical fermion states are antisymmetric.
For two electrons the overall state, including spin and space, must be antisymmetric.
A Slater determinant enforces antisymmetry and vanishes if two fermions occupy the same one-particle spin-orbital.
workflow: Transform to center-of-mass and relative coordinates if the Hamiltonian permits.
State whether the particles are distinguishable, identical bosons, or identical fermions.
Build the required symmetric or antisymmetric combination, including spin, then normalize.

formulas.name: Two-body reduction
formulas.latex: \mathbf R=\frac{m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2}{M},\quad \mathbf r=\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2,\quad \mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{M}
formulas.plain: R is center of mass; r is relative position; reduced mass mu = m1 m2/(m1+m2)
conditions: Two particles with interaction V(|r1-r2|).
checks: For a very heavy second particle, mu approaches m1.

formulas.name: Exchange symmetrization
formulas.plain: two-particle state is normalized symmetric plus or antisymmetric minus combination
conditions: Two normalized one-particle states; plus for bosons or a symmetric sector, minus for fermions or an antisymmetric sector.
checks: The antisymmetric state vanishes when a=b.

formulas.name: Slater determinant
formulas.plain: fermion N-body state = 1/sqrt(N factorial) times determinant of occupied spin-orbitals
conditions: N identical fermions in orthonormal spin-orbitals.
checks: Exchanging two particle labels changes the sign.

formulas.name: Two-spin singlet and triplet
formulas.plain: singlet m=0 is antisymmetric minus combination; triplet m=0 is symmetric plus combination
conditions: Two spin-one-half particles.
checks: The singlet has one state; the triplet has three.

commonTraps: Antisymmetrizing only the spatial part while ignoring spin.
Using the Pauli principle for distinguishable particles.
Forgetting overlap terms when normalizing combinations of nonorthogonal orbitals.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Matrix mechanics, basis changes, and density operators
familyPatterns: 11.3 Unitary and Similarity Transformations in Quantum Mechanics
recognition: Use matrices when the Hilbert space is finite or truncated, when changing representations, or when a statistical mixture or subsystem cannot be described by one state vector.
keyIdeas: Matrix elements are operator actions expressed in a chosen basis; physical eigenvalues and expectation values are basis independent.
Unitary transformations preserve inner products.
A density operator describes both pure states and classical mixtures; tracing out an entangled partner can create a mixed reduced state.
workflow: Declare the ordered basis before writing any matrix.
Transform the state and operator consistently or work with basis-invariant traces.
Check Hermiticity, unit trace, and nonnegative eigenvalues for any density matrix.

formulas.name: Matrix elements
formulas.plain: matrix element A_mn = bra m A ket n

variables.meaning: row m, column n matrix element

conditions: Chosen orthonormal basis.
checks: For Hermitian A, A_mn equals complex conjugate of A_nm.

formulas.name: Unitary basis transformation
formulas.plain: new coordinates of state = U dagger old state; new operator matrix = U dagger A U

variables.meaning: unitary matrix whose columns encode the new basis in the old basis

conditions: Passive basis change under the stated column convention.
checks: Eigenvalues and expectation values are unchanged.

formulas.name: Density operator
formulas.plain: rho = weighted sum of state projectors; trace rho = 1
conditions: Positive semidefinite ensemble density operator.
checks: All eigenvalues are nonnegative and sum to one.

formulas.name: Density-matrix expectation and purity
formulas.plain: mean A = trace(rho A); purity equals one for a pure state
conditions: Finite or trace-class density operator; mixed states have purity below one.
checks: For a d-dimensional maximally mixed state, purity is 1/d.

formulas.name: Reduced state
formulas.plain: state of subsystem A = partial trace over subsystem B
conditions: Composite Hilbert space A tensor B.
checks: The reduced state still has unit trace.

commonTraps: Writing a matrix without specifying basis order.
Transforming an operator but not the state, or vice versa.
Assuming every mixed reduced state represents mere ignorance rather than entanglement.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Electromagnetic coupling, gauge phase, and magnetic orbital motion
familyPatterns: 10.4 A Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field
Minimal coupling, gauge phase, and the Aharonov-Bohm effect
recognition: Use minimal coupling when scalar or vector electromagnetic potentials enter the Hamiltonian, especially for magnetic fields, gauge transformations, Landau levels, or flux-dependent phase.
keyIdeas: Canonical momentum p and mechanical momentum p-qA differ in a magnetic field.
Gauge-dependent potentials change the wavefunction phase while gauge-invariant probabilities and fields remain unchanged.
A confined magnetic flux can shift an interference phase even where the local magnetic field along the paths is zero.
workflow: Specify charge q, scalar potential phi, vector potential A, and gauge.
