Build the Hamiltonian from mechanical momentum p-qA and exploit translational or rotational symmetry.
Express final observables using B, electric field, or a closed-loop phase.

formulas.name: Minimal-coupling Hamiltonian
formulas.plain: H = (p - q A) squared/(2m) + q scalar-potential
conditions: Nonrelativistic spinless charged particle; add spin magnetic coupling when applicable.
checks: Mechanical momentum is p-qA.
The Hamiltonian has energy units.

formulas.name: Gauge transformation
formulas.plain: A changes by grad chi; scalar potential changes by minus time derivative chi; psi gains phase exp(i q chi/hbar)
conditions: Consistent electromagnetic gauge transformation.
checks: Electric and magnetic fields are unchanged.

formulas.name: Aharonov-Bohm phase
formulas.plain: phase shift = q/hbar times closed integral A dot dl = q magnetic flux/hbar
conditions: Coherent paths enclosing flux; local force along the field-free paths need not be present.
checks: Phase is dimensionless and periodic modulo 2 pi.

formulas.name: Cyclotron and Landau scales
formulas.plain: cyclotron frequency = absolute q B/m; orbital Landau energy = hbar omega_c(n+1/2)
conditions: Uniform magnetic field, free transverse orbital motion, nonrelativistic spinless spectrum; longitudinal kinetic energy and spin may add.
checks: Level spacing is proportional to B.

commonTraps: Replacing canonical momentum by mv without accounting for A.
Changing A without changing the wavefunction phase.
Claiming the Aharonov-Bohm effect requires a classical magnetic force along the particle paths.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Atomic transitions, selection rules, and lasers
familyPatterns: 7-8 Excited States and Spectra of Atoms
recognition: Use transition and rate ideas when light drives or accompanies changes between atomic states, when a line is allowed or forbidden, or when stimulated emission and population inversion appear.
keyIdeas: The transition frequency follows the energy difference, while the transition strength follows a matrix element.
Electric-dipole selection rules are consequences of parity and angular momentum, not absolute bans on every higher-order process.
Laser gain requires stimulated emission to exceed losses, usually through population inversion.
workflow: Find the initial and final energies and quantum numbers.
Test the relevant interaction matrix element or its selection rules.
Separate the line frequency from the transition probability or rate.

formulas.name: Transition frequency
formulas.plain: hbar omega_fi = absolute energy difference

variables.meaning: angular frequency of absorbed or emitted radiation

conditions: Energy-conserving transition between well-defined levels.
checks: Frequency is positive.

formulas.name: Electric-dipole matrix element
formulas.plain: transition dipole = charge times matrix element of position between final and initial states
conditions: Long-wavelength electric-dipole approximation.
checks: If symmetry makes the matrix element zero, the electric-dipole transition is forbidden at this order.

formulas.name: Common electric-dipole rules
formulas.plain: electric dipole: delta l plus or minus one, delta m zero or plus/minus one, spin unchanged

variables.meaning: orbital, magnetic, and spin quantum numbers

conditions: One-electron-like orbital selection in the electric-dipole approximation; polarization further restricts delta m.
checks: Parity changes for an electric-dipole transition.

formulas.name: Einstein rate balance
formulas.plain: absorption, stimulated emission, and spontaneous emission rates use B12 rho N1, B21 rho N2, and A21 N2
conditions: Two-level rate model.
checks: Stimulated rates scale with radiation density; spontaneous emission does not.

commonTraps: Using an energy difference alone to infer transition intensity.
Calling a dipole-forbidden line impossible rather than suppressed at that order.
Confusing a metastable upper level with population inversion by itself.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Time-independent nondegenerate perturbation theory
recognition: Use nondegenerate perturbation theory when H=H0+lambda V, the unperturbed eigenstate is isolated, and the perturbation is weak compared with relevant level spacings.
keyIdeas: First-order energy is the diagonal expectation of the perturbation.
State mixing is controlled by off-diagonal matrix elements divided by energy gaps.
A small perturbation operator is not enough; near degeneracy can invalidate the nondegenerate expansion.
workflow: Identify the unperturbed eigenstates, energies, and any degeneracy.
Use symmetry to eliminate matrix elements.
Compute energy corrections before state corrections and check the size of every mixing ratio.

formulas.name: Perturbation expansion
formulas.plain: H = H0 + lambda V; energy = unperturbed plus first, second, and higher corrections

variables.meaning: bookkeeping parameter set to one after ordering terms

conditions: Analytic weak-coupling expansion around an isolated unperturbed level.
checks: Every correction term has energy units after its lambda power is included.

formulas.name: First-order energy
formulas.plain: first-order energy = diagonal expectation of V in unperturbed state n
conditions: Normalized nondegenerate unperturbed eigenstate.
checks: A parity-odd perturbation has zero first-order shift in a parity eigenstate.

formulas.name: First-order state correction
formulas.plain: first-order state = sum over other states of V_mn divided by energy gap times state m
conditions: Intermediate normalization with the first-order correction orthogonal to the original state.
checks: Mixing is dimensionless.
Small denominators warn of degeneracy.

formulas.name: Second-order energy
formulas.plain: second-order energy = sum of squared coupling matrix elements over signed energy gaps
conditions: Discrete nondegenerate spectrum; continuum contributions become integrals.
checks: The ground-state second-order correction is nonpositive when all coupled states lie above it.

commonTraps: Using nondegenerate formulas inside a degenerate subspace.
Dropping the sign of the energy denominator.
Forgetting that the perturbation may also change eigenvectors even when the first-order energy shift vanishes.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Degenerate perturbations, Stark shifts, and nearly free electrons
recognition: Use degenerate perturbation theory when multiple unperturbed states share an energy or are close enough that ordinary mixing denominators become large.
keyIdeas: The correct zeroth-order states are eigenvectors of the perturbation restricted to the degenerate subspace.
Linear Stark splitting occurs when parity-degenerate states can mix; otherwise the leading shift can be quadratic.
A periodic potential mixes degenerate plane waves at a Brillouin-zone boundary and opens an energy gap.
workflow: Build the perturbation matrix W_ab within each degenerate subspace.
Diagonalize W before coupling to states outside that subspace.
Use symmetry to block-diagonalize and interpret the resulting splittings.

formulas.name: Secular equation
formulas.plain: W_ab is the perturbation matrix in the degenerate subspace; its eigenvalues are first-order shifts

variables.meaning: basis states in one degenerate eigenspace

conditions: Exact unperturbed degeneracy.
checks: The number of first-order branches equals the subspace dimension.

formulas.name: Electric-field perturbation
formulas.plain: electric perturbation = minus dipole dot field = q E dot r
conditions: Uniform static electric field; sign follows the particle charge and chosen potential convention.
checks: A nondegenerate parity eigenstate has zero permanent dipole expectation.

formulas.name: Quadratic Stark form
formulas.plain: quadratic Stark shift = -one half polarizability times field squared
conditions: Leading response when the linear shift vanishes and the field is weak.
checks: For a stable ground state alpha is typically positive, lowering the energy.

formulas.name: Nearly free-electron gap
formulas.plain: at a two-state Bragg degeneracy, energies split by plus or minus |V_G| and the gap is 2|V_G|

variables.meaning: Fourier component of the periodic potential coupling the degenerate waves

conditions: Weak periodic potential and an isolated two-wave degeneracy.
checks: The gap vanishes with the periodic coupling.

commonTraps: Keeping an arbitrary basis inside a degenerate space and calling diagonal entries the shifts.
Predicting a linear Stark effect without checking parity and degeneracy.
Opening a band gap away from the wave-vector degeneracy where the states do not strongly mix.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Time-dependent perturbations, resonance, and transition rates
familyPatterns: Time-dependent perturbations, transition rates, and Fermi's golden rule
recognition: Use time-dependent perturbation theory when a weak external interaction is switched, pulsed, or oscillated and the question asks for transition amplitudes or rates.
keyIdeas: Transitions require a nonzero coupling matrix element and frequency content near the energy gap.
A finite pulse produces a finite-width resonance; the infinite-time limit produces an energy-conserving delta function.
Fermi's golden rule applies to a continuum or dense set of final states, not a lone exactly resonant two-level system for all times.
workflow: Expand in unperturbed energy eigenstates and transform to the interaction picture.
Compute the time integral of the matrix element with its phase factor.
Square only after summing coherent amplitudes; convert to a rate only in the appropriate long-time continuum limit.

formulas.name: First-order transition amplitude
formulas.plain: first-order amplitude = -i/hbar integral of V_fi(t) exp(i omega_fi t) dt
conditions: Weak perturbation, initial unperturbed eigenstate i, first order.
checks: Amplitude is dimensionless.
At t=0 the transition amplitude is zero.

formulas.name: Finite-time resonance factor
formulas.plain: squared finite-time phase integral = 4 sin squared(detuning times t/2)/detuning squared
conditions: Constant-amplitude Fourier component over a rectangular time window.
checks: At exact resonance the limiting value is t squared.

formulas.name: Fermi golden rule
formulas.plain: transition rate = 2 pi/hbar times coupling squared times density of final states

variables.meaning: density of accessible final states per energy

conditions: Weak coupling, long-enough time, slowly varying continuum density and matrix element.
checks: Units are inverse time.

formulas.name: Two-level Rabi frequency on resonance
formulas.plain: on-resonance Rabi angular frequency = coupling/hbar; transition probability oscillates as sin squared

variables.meaning: Rabi angular frequency under the stated coupling convention

conditions: Coherent resonant two-level system in the rotating-wave approximation; factor conventions vary with how the drive amplitude is defined.
checks: Probability remains between zero and one and returns periodically.

commonTraps: Using a probability amplitude as a probability.
Replacing a finite-time sinc-squared line by a delta function too early.
Applying the golden rule where coherent two-level oscillations are required.

topics.subject: Quantum Mechanics
topics.title: Quantum statistics and many-body applications
familyPatterns: 12.8 Brief Description of Quantum Models for Superconductivity and Superfluidity
Applications to atomic, molecular, solid-state, nuclear, and quantum-statistical systems
recognition: Use Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac occupation laws when indistinguishable particles share thermal single-particle states, and use symmetry plus collective-state ideas for qualitative superfluid or superconducting models.
keyIdeas: Bosons may macroscopically occupy one state; fermion occupation is limited by the exclusion principle.
The chemical potential enforces mean particle number and must respect the allowed range for the chosen statistics.
Superfluidity and superconductivity are collective quantum phenomena; a one-particle formula alone does not explain them.
workflow: Identify boson versus fermion, conserved particle number, temperature, and density of states.
Use the appropriate mean occupation and integrate over states for total number or energy.
Check classical and zero-temperature limits before interpreting a collective result.

formulas.name: Bose-Einstein occupation
formulas.plain: mean boson occupation = 1/[exp((energy-mu)/(k_B T))-1]
conditions: Ideal bosons in grand-canonical equilibrium; mu does not exceed the lowest single-particle energy.
checks: Occupation can exceed one.

formulas.name: Fermi-Dirac occupation
formulas.plain: mean fermion occupation = 1/[exp((energy-mu)/(k_B T))+1]

variables.meaning: mean occupation of one fermionic state

conditions: Ideal fermions in grand-canonical equilibrium.
checks: Occupation lies between zero and one.
At zero temperature it becomes a step at the Fermi energy.

formulas.name: Thermal state count
formulas.plain: particle number = integral of density of states times mean occupation
conditions: Continuum approximation; add separately occupied discrete states when necessary.
checks: Density of states times d energy is a number of states.

formulas.name: Classical dilute limit
formulas.plain: both BE and FD occupations approach the Boltzmann factor in the dilute limit
conditions: Mean occupation much less than one.
checks: Quantum plus or minus one becomes negligible compared with the exponential.

commonTraps: Using Bose-Einstein statistics for half-integer-spin identical particles.
Allowing a Fermi state occupation above one.
Treating superconductivity as ordinary single-electron conduction without pairing and coherence.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Temperature, equilibrium, and thermometry
recognition: Two systems exchange energy until a measurable state variable becomes equal.
A problem converts temperature scales or calibrates a thermometer.
keyIdeas: Temperature labels the direction of spontaneous thermal energy transfer.
The zeroth law makes temperature a consistent state variable.
Temperature differences convert differently from absolute temperatures.
workflow: Identify the systems and what can cross their boundary.
Convert to kelvin before using ratios or thermodynamic formulas.
Apply equilibrium only after checking that the relevant exchange is allowed.

formulas.name: Celsius–kelvin conversion
conditions: Use kelvin in ratios, logarithms, exponentials, and gas laws.
checks: A physical absolute temperature cannot be negative.

formulas.name: Fahrenheit–Celsius conversion
conditions: For temperature differences, ΔT_F = (9/5)ΔT_C; do not add 32.
checks: 0 °C maps to 32 °F and 100 °C maps to 212 °F.

commonTraps: Using Celsius in a temperature ratio.
Assuming equilibrium when a constraint blocks heat, volume, or particle exchange.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Thermal expansion and thermal stress
recognition: A solid or fluid changes size with temperature.
Expansion is constrained and therefore produces stress.
keyIdeas: Linear expansion is first order in temperature change for modest ranges.
For isotropic solids the volume coefficient is approximately three times the linear coefficient.
Constraint converts the free thermal strain into mechanical stress.
workflow: Compute the unconstrained thermal strain.
Apply geometry or compatibility constraints.
Use elasticity only for the strain that is prevented.

formulas.name: Linear expansion
formulas.plain: ΔL = α L_0 ΔT
conditions: α is approximately constant over the stated temperature range.
checks: Expansion has the sign of αΔT.

formulas.name: Volume expansion
formulas.latex: ΔV = β V_0 ΔT, with β ≈ 3α
formulas.plain: ΔV = β V_0 ΔT, with β ≈ 3α
conditions: β≈3α for an isotropic solid and small strain.
checks: Both sides have units of volume.

formulas.name: Fully constrained thermal stress
formulas.plain: σ = -Y α ΔT
conditions: One-dimensional, linear-elastic, fully constrained expansion.
checks: Heating under full constraint produces compression.

commonTraps: Using final instead of reference length inconsistently.
Applying σ=YαΔT when the body is only partly constrained.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Heat capacity, calorimetry, and phase change
recognition: Bodies at different temperatures are brought into thermal contact.
Heating crosses a phase boundary.
keyIdeas: Sensible heating changes temperature; latent heating changes phase at nearly fixed temperature.
For an isolated calorimeter, energy lost by hot parts equals energy gained by cold parts.
Heat capacity depends on the thermodynamic constraint.
workflow: Choose a final-state hypothesis, including which phases remain.
Write one signed energy term for each temperature interval and phase change.
Set the total energy transfer to zero for an isolated assembly and check the phase assumption.

formulas.name: Sensible heat
formulas.latex: Q = m c ΔT = C ΔT
formulas.plain: Q = m c ΔT = C ΔT
conditions: No phase change and c approximately constant.
checks: Q has units of energy and follows the sign of ΔT for energy entering the object.

formulas.name: Latent heat
formulas.plain: Q = m L
conditions: Phase change at the transition temperature.
checks: Temperature remains fixed during an ideal equilibrium phase change.

formulas.name: Isolated calorimetry
formulas.plain: Σ_i Q_i = 0
conditions: Negligible energy exchange with the surroundings.
checks: Every energy loss must appear as another component’s gain.

commonTraps: Averaging initial temperatures without heat-capacity weights.
Continuing a temperature ramp through a phase change without a latent-heat plateau.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Conduction, convection, and radiation
recognition: The question asks for a heat-transfer rate or steady temperature profile.
Several heat-loss mechanisms act in parallel or layers act in series.
keyIdeas: Thermal resistance organizes steady one-dimensional conduction.
Net radiation is a difference of fourth powers in absolute temperature.
Steady state means equal rate through series layers, not zero rate.
workflow: Sketch the thermal circuit and boundary temperatures.
Combine series resistances or parallel heat-loss channels.
Use absolute temperature for radiation and verify the direction of flow.

formulas.name: One-dimensional conduction
formulas.plain: P = k A (T_hot - T_cold)/L
conditions: Steady, one-dimensional flow with constant k.
checks: Power is positive from hot to cold.

formulas.name: Thermal resistance
formulas.plain: R_th = L/(kA), so P = ΔT/R_th
conditions: Series layers share one heat rate; add their resistances.
checks: R_th has units K/W.

formulas.name: Net thermal radiation
formulas.plain: P_net = ε σ A (T^4 - T_env^4)
conditions: Temperatures are absolute and surfaces are treated with an effective emissivity.
checks: If T=T_env, the net radiative power is zero.

commonTraps: Using Celsius in T^4.
Adding conductivities rather than thermal resistances for layers in series.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Equations of state and ideal gases
recognition: Pressure, volume, amount, and temperature specify an equilibrium gas state.
A real-gas correction is requested.
keyIdeas: An equation of state constrains equilibrium state variables; it does not specify a path.
Use per-particle k_B or per-mole R consistently.
Real-gas parameters represent attractions and excluded volume.
workflow: Choose particle or mole notation.
Write the equation of state at each equilibrium endpoint.
Use an additional process relation before connecting endpoints.

formulas.name: Ideal-gas equation
formulas.latex: PV = N k_B T = n R T
formulas.plain: PV = N k_B T = n R T
conditions: Dilute gas with negligible interactions and classical statistics.
checks: PV and Nk_BT both have units of energy.

formulas.name: van der Waals equation
formulas.plain: (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT
conditions: Phenomenological real-gas model away from regimes where it fails.
checks: As a,b→0, recover PV=nRT.

commonTraps: Mixing N with R or n with k_B.
Trying to calculate work from endpoints alone.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Kinetic theory and molecular speeds
recognition: A macroscopic gas quantity must be related to molecular motion.
The problem asks for rms, mean, or most-probable speed.
keyIdeas: Pressure arises from momentum transfer at walls.
Temperature controls mean translational kinetic energy, not one molecule’s exact speed.
Different characteristic speeds are not interchangeable.
workflow: Identify the required average.
Use isotropy to replace one Cartesian component by one third of the total.
Check the scaling v∝sqrt(T/m).

formulas.name: Kinetic pressure
conditions: Dilute, isotropic ideal gas.
checks: The right side has units of pressure.

formulas.name: Mean translational energy
formulas.plain: <K_trans> = (3/2) k_B T

variables.meaning: mean translational kinetic energy per molecule

conditions: Classical, nonrelativistic ideal gas.
checks: Energy is proportional to T and vanishes in the classical extrapolation T→0.

formulas.name: Root-mean-square speed
formulas.plain: v_rms = sqrt(3 k_B T/m)
conditions: Classical Maxwell distribution.
checks: Heavier molecules are slower at fixed T.

commonTraps: Using molar mass where a single-particle mass is required without converting.
Equating rms speed with average speed.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Equipartition, degrees of freedom, and heat capacity
recognition: A heat capacity is inferred from accessible molecular modes.
A mode freezes out as temperature decreases.
keyIdeas: Each independent quadratic energy term contributes k_BT/2 to the mean energy.
A harmonic vibrational mode has both kinetic and potential quadratic terms.
Quantum level spacing controls whether a mode is thermally active.
workflow: Count independent quadratic terms without double counting constraints.
Write U from active degrees of freedom.
Differentiate U with respect to T under the stated constraint.

formulas.name: Equipartition energy
formulas.plain: U = (f/2) N k_B T

variables.meaning: number of active quadratic degrees of freedom

conditions: Classical regime for each counted mode.
checks: Each added quadratic term raises C_V by Nk_B/2.

formulas.name: Ideal-gas heat capacities
formulas.plain: C_V = (f/2)Nk_B; C_P = C_V + Nk_B
conditions: Ideal gas with fixed active f.
checks: C_P-C_V=Nk_B and γ=C_P/C_V>1.

commonTraps: Counting a vibration as one quadratic term instead of two.
Using classical equipartition below the excitation temperature of a mode.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: First law, boundaries, and PV work
recognition: Energy enters or leaves a thermodynamic system as heat and/or work.
A PV path or cycle determines work.
keyIdeas: Internal energy is a state function; heat and work are path-dependent transfers.
With the convention W_by>0 for expansion, ΔU=Q-W_by.
The signed area under a quasistatic PV curve is work done by the gas.
workflow: Draw and label the system boundary.
State the work sign convention before substituting.
Compute W from the path, then use the first law for Q or ΔU.

formulas.name: First law
formulas.plain: ΔU = Q - W_by
conditions: This sheet uses the work-by-the-system convention.
checks: For a complete cycle ΔU=0, so Q_net=W_net.

formulas.name: Quasistatic PV work
formulas.plain: W_by = ∫_(V_i)^(V_f) P_ext dV

variables.meaning: external pressure matched by the system in a quasistatic path

conditions: Boundary work along a specified path.
checks: Expansion gives positive W_by; compression gives negative W_by.

formulas.name: Ideal-gas internal-energy change
formulas.plain: ΔU = n C_V,m ΔT

variables.meaning: molar heat capacity at constant volume

conditions: Ideal gas; C_V,m constant or interpreted inside an integral.
checks: For an ideal gas, ΔU depends only on ΔT.

commonTraps: Switching between work-on and work-by conventions mid-solution.
Using W=PΔV when pressure varies.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, and adiabatic paths
recognition: A process constraint fixes T, P, V, or Q.
An ideal gas follows a named reversible path.
keyIdeas: The process constraint determines which terms in the first law vanish or simplify.
A reversible adiabatic relation is stronger than merely Q=0.
Heat capacities connect heat to temperature only under their named constraints.
workflow: Translate the process word into a mathematical constraint.
Combine the constraint with the equation of state.
Use the first law and verify the PV-curve shape.

formulas.name: Reversible isothermal ideal-gas work
formulas.plain: W_by = nRT ln(V_f/V_i)
conditions: Ideal gas, constant T, quasistatic path.
checks: Expansion gives W_by>0 and ΔU=0.

formulas.name: Reversible adiabatic relations
formulas.plain: PV^γ = const; TV^(γ-1) = const
conditions: Ideal gas, quasistatic adiabatic process, fixed γ.
checks: An adiabatic expansion cools the gas.

formulas.name: Adiabatic work
formulas.plain: W_by = (P_iV_i - P_fV_f)/(γ - 1)
conditions: Same assumptions as the reversible adiabatic relations.
checks: For expansion, P_iV_i>P_fV_f and W_by>0.

commonTraps: Treating every adiabatic process as quasistatic.
Using the isothermal logarithm for a constant-pressure path.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Heat engines, refrigerators, and Carnot bounds
recognition: A cyclic device exchanges heat with hot and cold reservoirs and produces or consumes work.
The question asks for a maximum possible performance.
keyIdeas: A cycle returns the working substance to its initial state, so ΔU_cycle=0.
Efficiency and coefficient of performance answer different questions.
Carnot performance is an upper bound set only by reservoir temperatures.
workflow: Draw energy arrows and enforce Q_H=W+Q_C.
Choose efficiency, refrigerator COP, or heat-pump COP.
Compare the result with the reversible bound using kelvin.

formulas.name: Heat-engine efficiency
formulas.plain: η = W_out/Q_H = 1 - Q_C/Q_H
conditions: Cyclic heat engine; Q_H and Q_C denote positive magnitudes.
checks: 0≤η<1 for an ordinary engine.

formulas.name: Carnot efficiency
formulas.plain: η_C = 1 - T_C/T_H
conditions: Reversible engine between two reservoirs; temperatures in kelvin.
checks: η_C→0 as T_C→T_H.

formulas.name: Refrigerator and heat-pump COP
formulas.plain: COP_R = Q_C/W; COP_HP = Q_H/W = COP_R + 1
conditions: Cyclic device with positive heat/work magnitudes.
checks: COP can exceed one because it is not an efficiency.

formulas.name: Carnot refrigerator bound
formulas.plain: COP_R,C = T_C/(T_H - T_C)
conditions: Reversible refrigerator.
checks: COP worsens as the temperature lift grows.

commonTraps: Using Celsius in Carnot ratios.
Rejecting COP>1 as impossible.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Entropy, reversibility, and the second law
recognition: A problem asks whether a process is possible or spontaneous.
An entropy change must be computed along an irreversible process.
keyIdeas: Entropy is a state function, so calculate its change on any convenient reversible path.
For an isolated total system, entropy cannot decrease.
Equality corresponds to an ideal reversible process; real finite-gradient processes produce entropy.
workflow: Define system plus surroundings.
Compute each entropy change with a reversible surrogate.
Add all parts and test ΔS_universe≥0.

formulas.name: Entropy change
formulas.plain: ΔS = ∫_rev δQ/T
conditions: Integral is evaluated on a reversible path between the actual endpoints.
checks: Entropy has units J/K.

formulas.name: Clausius inequality
formulas.plain: ∮ δQ/T ≤ 0
conditions: Equality for a reversible cycle; strict inequality for an irreversible cycle.
checks: A one-reservoir cycle cannot convert all absorbed heat to work.

formulas.name: Second-law test
formulas.plain: ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0
conditions: System and relevant surroundings together are isolated.
checks: Negative total entropy signals an error or impossible process.

commonTraps: Writing ΔS=Q/T for an irreversible path with changing temperature.
Checking only the system entropy while ignoring the surroundings.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Entropy changes of ideal gases
familyPatterns: gas equations of state and entropy
recognition: An ideal gas moves between two equilibrium states and an entropy difference is requested.
A free expansion or mixing problem has Q=W=0 but ΔS≠0.
keyIdeas: Ideal-gas entropy depends on both temperature and volume (or temperature and pressure).
Free expansion changes no ideal-gas internal energy but increases accessible volume and entropy.
Mixing identical gases must not create a distinguishability entropy.
workflow: Choose endpoint variables with known values.
Use a reversible path formula even if the actual process is irreversible.
Check extensivity and the identical-gas limit.

formulas.name: Ideal-gas entropy change
formulas.latex: ΔS = n C_V,m ln(T_f/T_i) + nR ln(V_f/V_i)
formulas.plain: ΔS = n C_V,m ln(T_f/T_i) + nR ln(V_f/V_i)
conditions: Ideal gas with fixed particle number and approximately constant heat capacity.
checks: Isothermal expansion has ΔS=nR ln(V_f/V_i)>0.

formulas.name: Equivalent pressure form
formulas.latex: ΔS = n C_P,m ln(T_f/T_i) - nR ln(P_f/P_i)
formulas.plain: ΔS = n C_P,m ln(T_f/T_i) - nR ln(P_f/P_i)
conditions: Same assumptions as above.
checks: Both endpoint formulas must agree via PV=nRT.

commonTraps: Using a heat integral along the actual free-expansion path and concluding ΔS=0.
Creating entropy on removing a partition between identical gases at the same state.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Microstates, multiplicity, probability, and Stirling approximation
recognition: A macrostate can be realized by many microscopic arrangements.
Factorials or sharply peaked probability distributions appear.
keyIdeas: For equal a priori microstates, macrostate probability is proportional to multiplicity.
Independent subsystems multiply multiplicities and therefore add entropies.
Large-N distributions are extraordinarily concentrated near equilibrium.
workflow: Define the macrostate variables and constraints.
Count compatible microstates without double counting.
Use logarithms and Stirling approximation before evaluating huge factorials.

formulas.name: Boltzmann entropy
formulas.plain: S = k_B ln Ω
conditions: Equal weighting of accessible microstates in the isolated description.
checks: Products of multiplicities become sums of entropy.

formulas.name: Binomial multiplicity

variables.meaning: number in one of two states

conditions: Two-state objects with fixed counts.
checks: Ω is largest near n=N/2.

formulas.name: Stirling approximation
formulas.latex: ln N! ≈ N ln N - N + (1/2)ln(2πN)
formulas.plain: ln N! ≈ N ln N - N + (1/2)ln(2πN)
conditions: Use leading terms when N is large; retain correction when accuracy matters.
checks: The logarithm avoids overflow and exposes extensive scaling.

commonTraps: Adding multiplicities for independent subsystems instead of multiplying them.
Dropping constraints when counting accessible states.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Einstein solids and energy exchange
recognition: Energy quanta are distributed among harmonic oscillators.
Two solids exchange a fixed total number of quanta.
keyIdeas: Multiplicity counts weak compositions of q indistinguishable quanta among N distinguishable oscillators.
The equilibrium macrostate maximizes the product Ω_AΩ_B.
Heat flows toward the subsystem with larger entropy slope 1/T.
workflow: Write Ω for each solid.
Use q_A+q_B=q_total.
Maximize lnΩ_total or compare multiplicity ratios.

formulas.name: Einstein-solid multiplicity
conditions: Noninteracting identical-frequency oscillators; total q fixed.

formulas.name: Composite multiplicity
formulas.plain: Ω_total(q_A) = Ω_A(N_A,q_A) Ω_B(N_B,q_total-q_A)
conditions: Weakly coupled subsystems with fixed total energy.
checks: The most probable split maximizes lnΩ_total.

commonTraps: Treating oscillators as indistinguishable in the counting.
Maximizing Ω_A+Ω_B rather than Ω_AΩ_B.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Two-state paramagnets
recognition: Independent magnetic moments occupy two energy levels.
Magnetization or heat capacity is requested as a function of field and temperature.
keyIdeas: The field splits two spin energies and biases their populations.
Magnetization follows an odd tanh response.
The two-level heat capacity vanishes at both low and high temperature and peaks between.
workflow: Choose the sign convention for energies.
Build the one-spin partition function.
Differentiate ln Z for energy and with respect to field for magnetization.

formulas.name: One-spin partition function
formulas.plain: z = 2 cosh(β μ_m B)
conditions: Independent two-state moments with energies ∓μ_mB.
checks: At B=0, z=2.

formulas.name: Paramagnet magnetization
formulas.latex: M = N μ_m tanh(β μ_m B)
formulas.plain: M = N μ_m tanh(β μ_m B)
conditions: Independent noninteracting moments.
checks: M saturates at ±Nμ_m and is linear for weak field.

formulas.name: Two-level heat capacity
formulas.latex: C = Nk_B x^2 sech^2(x), x=β μ_m B
formulas.plain: C = Nk_B x^2 sech^2(x), x=β μ_m B
conditions: Same two-level model.
checks: C→0 as x→0 and as x→∞.

commonTraps: Losing the sign in E=-μ·B.
Assuming equipartition applies to a bounded two-level spectrum.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Temperature, pressure, and chemical potential from entropy
recognition: An intensive variable must be derived from S(U,V,N).
Two subsystems exchange energy, volume, or particles.
keyIdeas: Equilibrium maximizes total entropy under the allowed exchange.
The entropy derivatives define T, P, and μ.
The exchanged quantity determines which intensive variable equalizes.
workflow: Write the conserved total quantity.
Differentiate S_total for a small transfer.
Set the first variation to zero and inspect the second variation for stability.

formulas.name: Entropy representation
formulas.plain: dS = (1/T)dU + (P/T)dV - (μ/T)dN
conditions: Simple compressible one-component system.
checks: Each coefficient is an entropy derivative with other extensive variables fixed.

formulas.name: Derivative definitions
conditions: Equilibrium thermodynamics.
checks: Energy exchange equalizes T; volume exchange equalizes P; particle exchange equalizes μ.

commonTraps: Forgetting the minus sign in the chemical-potential derivative.
Equalizing pressure across a rigid wall that cannot move.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Thermodynamic potentials and natural variables
recognition: The environment fixes T, P, or both, so entropy maximization is inconvenient.
A problem asks for available work or an equilibrium criterion.
keyIdeas: Legendre transforms exchange inconvenient extensive natural variables for controlled intensive ones.
At fixed T,V, equilibrium minimizes F; at fixed T,P, it minimizes G.
A potential’s differential reveals its natural variables and derivative identities.
workflow: Identify the controlled environmental variables.
Choose U, H, F, or G whose natural variables match them.
Differentiate the potential or compare it between candidate states.

formulas.name: Fundamental thermodynamic identity
formulas.latex: dU = T dS - P dV + μ dN
formulas.plain: dU = T dS - P dV + μ dN
conditions: Simple compressible one-component system.
checks: Signs match work done by expansion.

formulas.name: Helmholtz free energy
formulas.plain: F=U-TS; dF=-S dT-P dV+μ dN
conditions: Equilibrium states; simple compressible system.
checks: Natural variables are T,V,N.

formulas.name: Gibbs free energy
formulas.plain: G=U+PV-TS; dG=-S dT+V dP+μ dN
conditions: Equilibrium states; simple compressible system.
checks: Natural variables are T,P,N.

formulas.name: Enthalpy
formulas.plain: H=U+PV; dH=T dS+V dP+μ dN
conditions: Equilibrium states.
checks: At fixed pressure with only PV work, heat equals ΔH for a quasistatic process.

commonTraps: Minimizing the wrong potential for the imposed constraints.
Treating F or G as the energy rather than a Legendre-transformed state function.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Maxwell relations and response functions
recognition: A difficult-to-measure entropy derivative must be rewritten in terms of P,V,T.
Heat capacities, compressibilities, and expansion coefficients are linked.
keyIdeas: Equality of mixed partial derivatives generates Maxwell relations.
Always derive the needed relation from the correct potential instead of memorizing signs blindly.
Thermodynamic stability constrains response functions such as heat capacity and compressibility.
workflow: Write the differential of a potential with matching natural variables.
Identify the two first derivatives.
Equate crossed second derivatives and preserve held-fixed variables.

formulas.name: Maxwell relation from F
conditions: F(T,V,N) is twice differentiable and N is fixed.
checks: Both sides describe thermal-mechanical coupling.

formulas.name: Maxwell relation from G
conditions: G(T,P,N) is twice differentiable and N is fixed.
checks: The minus sign follows from dG=-S dT+V dP.

formulas.name: Heat-capacity difference
formulas.plain: C_P - C_V = T V α^2/κ_T
conditions: Stable simple compressible system.
checks: Right side is nonnegative for κ_T>0, so C_P≥C_V.

commonTraps: Dropping the fixed-variable subscripts.
Memorizing a Maxwell sign without reconstructing the potential differential.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Boltzmann factors and canonical probabilities
recognition: A small system exchanges energy with a heat reservoir at fixed temperature.
Discrete energy levels and thermal probabilities are given or sought.
keyIdeas: The reservoir converts total multiplicity into an exponential weight e^{-βE}.
The partition function normalizes probabilities.
Energy gaps matter only through the dimensionless ratio ΔE/(k_BT).
workflow: List energies and degeneracies.
Form unnormalized weights g_i e^{-βE_i}.
Normalize by Z and compute requested averages.

formulas.name: Canonical probability
formulas.plain: p_i = g_i e^(-βE_i)/Z
conditions: System weakly coupled to a large heat reservoir.
checks: Probabilities sum to one and are unchanged by shifting all energies by a constant.

formulas.name: Partition function
formulas.plain: Z = Σ_i g_i e^(-βE_i)
conditions: Sum over all accessible energy levels.
checks: Z is dimensionless when degeneracies are dimensionless.

formulas.name: Thermal average
formulas.plain: <A> = Σ_i p_i A_i

variables.meaning: value of observable in state i

conditions: Observable is diagonal in the sampled state description or a classical discrete variable.
checks: A constant observable averages to the same constant.

commonTraps: Forgetting degeneracy factors.
Using β=k_BT instead of β=1/(k_BT).

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Partition functions and thermodynamic derivatives
recognition: A partition function is known and macroscopic thermodynamics is requested.
Heat capacity or energy fluctuations must be extracted without summing again.
keyIdeas: ln Z is the generating function for canonical thermodynamics.
Differentiation with respect to β brings down energy.
Fluctuations link microscopic variance to positive heat capacity.
workflow: Simplify ln Z before differentiating.
Hold volume and particle number fixed unless stated otherwise.
Check high- and low-temperature limits.

formulas.name: Mean energy from Z
formulas.plain: U = -∂ ln Z/∂β
conditions: Canonical ensemble at fixed V,N.
checks: Increasing β corresponds to lowering temperature.

formulas.name: Helmholtz free energy from Z
formulas.plain: F = -k_B T ln Z
conditions: Canonical ensemble.
checks: A dimensionless Z makes the logarithm valid.

formulas.name: Entropy from Z
formulas.plain: S = k_B(ln Z + βU)
conditions: Canonical ensemble.
checks: For one certain state, Z=e^{-βE} and S=0.

formulas.name: Energy fluctuation relation
formulas.plain: C_V = Var(E)/(k_B T^2)
conditions: Canonical ensemble.
checks: Variance is nonnegative, so canonical C_V≥0.

commonTraps: Differentiating Z instead of ln Z without the 1/Z factor.
Letting temperature-dependent energy levels vary inside a derivative without accounting for it.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Composite partition functions and the ideal gas
recognition: Independent subsystems or particles make a many-body partition function.
Classical identical particles require the Gibbs correction.
keyIdeas: Independent degrees of freedom multiply partition functions and add ln Z.
The factor 1/N! corrects classical overcounting of identical-particle label permutations.
The thermal wavelength sets the scale for quantum overlap.
workflow: Factor the Hamiltonian into independent pieces.
Build the one-particle translational/internal partition function.
Apply the identical-particle factor and test the dilute condition nλ_T^3≪1.

formulas.name: Independent subsystems
formulas.plain: Z_total = ∏_a Z_a

variables.meaning: partition function of independent part a

conditions: Hamiltonian is additive and states factorize.
checks: ln Z_total is the sum of ln Z_a.

formulas.name: Thermal de Broglie wavelength
formulas.plain: λ_T = h/sqrt(2π m k_B T)
conditions: Nonrelativistic translational motion.
checks: λ_T grows at low temperature and for light particles.

formulas.name: Classical monatomic ideal-gas partition function
conditions: Dilute, noninteracting, identical monatomic particles.
checks: Dimensionless ratio V/λ_T^3 counts translational states.

commonTraps: Omitting 1/N! for identical classical particles.
Multiplying energies when independent partition functions should multiply.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Phase equilibrium, latent heat, and Clapeyron relation
recognition: Two phases coexist while pressure and temperature change.
The slope of a coexistence line or latent heat is requested.
keyIdeas: Coexisting phases have equal temperature, pressure, and chemical potential.
The Clapeyron slope comes from differentiating equality of chemical potentials.
First-order transitions have latent heat and a discontinuity in entropy or volume.
workflow: State μ_α=μ_β along coexistence.
Use dμ=-s dT+v dP for each phase.
Solve for dP/dT and inspect the sign using Δv.

formulas.name: Clapeyron equation
formulas.plain: dP/dT = Δs/Δv = L/(T Δv)

variables.meaning: latent heat per particle or mole

conditions: Two phases in equilibrium along a first-order coexistence curve; units used consistently.
checks: The slope sign follows the sign of Δv for positive L.

formulas.name: Chemical-potential differential
formulas.plain: dμ = -s dT + v dP
conditions: One-component phase at equilibrium.
checks: Units of both terms are energy per particle or mole.

commonTraps: Mixing total latent heat with molar volume change.
Assuming every coexistence curve has positive slope.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Mixtures, osmotic pressure, and colligative effects
recognition: Several species share a phase or a semipermeable membrane.
A property depends mainly on solute particle count.
keyIdeas: Each species has its own chemical potential.
Ideal mixing contributes a logarithm of concentration or mole fraction.
Osmotic pressure balances the solvent chemical-potential difference.
workflow: Identify which species can cross each boundary.
Write chemical potentials in each phase.
Set the transferable species’ chemical potentials equal and solve.

formulas.name: Ideal-mixture chemical potential
formulas.latex: μ_i = μ_i°(T,P) + k_B T ln x_i
formulas.plain: μ_i = μ_i°(T,P) + k_B T ln x_i
conditions: Ideal mixture; per-particle convention. Use RT for molar chemical potentials.
checks: As x_i decreases, μ_i decreases.

formulas.name: Dilute osmotic pressure
formulas.plain: Π = c_s R T
conditions: Dilute ideal solution and semipermeable membrane.
checks: Same form as the ideal-gas pressure of solute particles.

commonTraps: Equalizing the chemical potential of a species that cannot cross the membrane.
Using mass concentration where molar concentration is required.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Chemical equilibrium and reaction extent
recognition: Species interconvert under a stoichiometric constraint.
An equilibrium constant or reaction direction is requested.
keyIdeas: At fixed T,P, a spontaneous reaction lowers G until the reaction Gibbs energy vanishes.
Stoichiometric coefficients determine how particle numbers change with reaction extent.
The equilibrium constant is controlled by standard-state free energy.
workflow: Write dN_i=ν_i dξ.
Form Δ_rG=Σ_iν_iμ_i.
Set Δ_rG=0 at equilibrium or use its sign for the spontaneous direction.

formulas.name: Reaction Gibbs energy
formulas.plain: Δ_r G = Σ_i ν_i μ_i
conditions: Fixed temperature and pressure.
checks: At equilibrium Δ_rG=0; its sign sets the favorable direction.

formulas.name: Equilibrium constant
formulas.plain: K = exp[-Δ_r G°/(RT)]
conditions: Activities use the same standard state as Δ_rG°.
checks: Dimensionless K requires dimensionless activities.

commonTraps: Using unsigned stoichiometric coefficients.
Putting dimensional concentrations directly inside logarithms without a standard state.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Particle exchange and the grand partition function
recognition: A small system can exchange both energy and particles with a reservoir.
Binding sites or single-particle states may be empty or occupied.
keyIdeas: Particle exchange adds the chemical-potential weight e^{βμN}.
The grand partition function sums over both energy states and particle number.
Mean occupancy follows from a derivative with respect to βμ or from normalized occupancy weights.
workflow: List every allowed occupancy and its energy and particle number.
Assign each state the weight exp[-β(E-μN)].
Normalize with Ξ and check the empty/fully occupied limits.

formulas.name: Grand partition function
formulas.latex: Ξ = Σ_states exp[-β(E-μN)] = Σ_N e^(βμN) Z_N
formulas.plain: Ξ = Σ_states exp[-β(E-μN)] = Σ_N e^(βμN) Z_N
conditions: System weakly coupled to heat and particle reservoirs at fixed T,V,μ.
checks: Every exponent is dimensionless; fixed-N canonical terms are recovered inside the sum.

formulas.name: Grand-canonical probability
formulas.plain: p_(E,N) = exp[-β(E-μN)]/Ξ

variables.meaning: probability of a state with energy E and particle number N

conditions: Grand-canonical equilibrium.
checks: Probabilities sum to one.

formulas.name: Mean particle number
formulas.plain: <N> = (1/β) ∂lnΞ/∂μ = ∂lnΞ/∂(βμ)
conditions: Temperature and volume fixed in the μ derivative.
checks: Increasing μ favors states with more particles.

commonTraps: Using e^{-β(E+μN)} instead of e^{-β(E-μN)}.
Omitting allowed empty states from a binding-site partition function.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac statistics
recognition: Identical particles occupy quantum single-particle states.
The Pauli principle or unlimited bosonic occupancy matters.
keyIdeas: Fermions allow at most one particle per one-particle state; bosons allow any occupancy.
The chemical potential controls mean occupation in the grand-canonical description.
Both distributions approach Maxwell–Boltzmann form when occupancy is dilute.
workflow: Identify particle statistics and level degeneracy.
Compute the exponent β(ε-μ).
Use the correct sign and test the classical limit.

formulas.name: Fermi–Dirac occupation
conditions: Noninteracting fermions in thermal and diffusive equilibrium.
checks: Occupation stays between zero and one.

formulas.name: Bose–Einstein occupation
conditions: Noninteracting bosons; μ does not exceed the ground-state energy.
checks: Occupation can be arbitrarily large.

formulas.name: Classical dilute limit
formulas.plain: <n(ε)> ≈ exp[-β(ε-μ)]
conditions: exp(β(ε-μ))≫1.
checks: Bose and Fermi signs become irrelevant.

commonTraps: Swapping the plus and minus signs.
Allowing a boson chemical potential above the ground-state energy.

topics.subject: Thermodynamics & Statistical Mechanics
topics.title: Degenerate Fermi gases and Bose condensation
recognition: Temperature is comparable to a quantum degeneracy scale.
A zero-temperature Fermi sea or condensate fraction is requested.
keyIdeas: At T=0, fermions fill all states up to the Fermi energy.
Fermi pressure persists without thermal motion in the classical sense.
Below T_c, excited boson states saturate and excess particles enter the ground state.
workflow: Compute number density and the appropriate degeneracy temperature.
Compare T with T_F or T_c.
Use the low-temperature or condensed-limit formulas only when justified.

formulas.name: Fermi wavevector and energy
conditions: Uniform, nonrelativistic, spin-1/2 ideal Fermi gas at T=0.
checks: E_F increases with density as n^(2/3).

formulas.name: Zero-temperature Fermi energy and pressure
conditions: Three-dimensional nonrelativistic ideal Fermi gas at T=0.

formulas.name: Ideal-gas BEC critical temperature
conditions: Uniform three-dimensional noninteracting bosons.
checks: T_c rises with density and falls with mass.

formulas.name: Condensate fraction
conditions: Same ideal uniform gas for T<T_c.
checks: Fraction is one at T=0 and zero at T=T_c.

commonTraps: Using the spin-1/2 density relation for a different degeneracy without adjustment.
Calling every low-temperature boson system a condensate without comparing to T_c.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What four checks should follow any numerical mechanics answer?
flashcards.back: Dimensions, sign/direction, scale, and limiting behavior.
flashcards.reasoning: Algebra can be internally consistent while still describing the wrong quantity or an impossible regime.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What does a dot product select, and what does a cross product encode?
flashcards.back: The dot product selects parallel projection; the cross product gives perpendicular magnitude plus orientation.
flashcards.reasoning: This distinction identifies work/projection problems versus torque/angular-momentum problems.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: At a one-dimensional turning point, which quantity must be zero?
flashcards.back: Instantaneous velocity is zero; acceleration need not be.
flashcards.reasoning: A nonzero acceleration reverses the motion even though the object is momentarily at rest.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: When may the familiar constant-acceleration equations be used?
flashcards.back: Only over an interval where acceleration is constant.
flashcards.reasoning: They are integrated special cases of vdot=a, not universal definitions.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Why can a constant-speed particle still accelerate?
flashcards.back: Its velocity direction can change; curved motion has normal acceleration v squared over R.
flashcards.reasoning: Acceleration measures the vector change of velocity, not just change of speed.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What terms appear in planar polar acceleration?
flashcards.back: Radial: r-double-dot minus r phi-dot squared. Transverse: r phi-double-dot plus 2 r-dot phi-dot.
flashcards.reasoning: They arise because the polar unit vectors rotate as well as the components change.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What belongs on a free-body diagram?
flashcards.back: Only external forces acting on the chosen body or system, each with an identifiable agent.
flashcards.reasoning: Internal forces and forces exerted by the body belong to other diagrams or cancel within a larger system.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Do Newton's third-law forces cancel on one object's free-body diagram?
flashcards.back: No. They act on different bodies.
flashcards.reasoning: They cancel only when both bodies are included in a system momentum balance.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Is static friction always mu_s times N?
flashcards.back: No. Its magnitude adjusts from zero up to mu_s N.
flashcards.reasoning: The equality holds only at impending slip.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How do you obtain acceleration relations for an ideal string?
flashcards.back: Write its total length as a constant, then differentiate twice.
flashcards.reasoning: The pulley geometry, not intuition, determines signs and multiplicative factors.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is terminal velocity?
flashcards.back: A stable velocity at which the net force and acceleration vanish.
flashcards.reasoning: Velocity remains nonzero because drag balances the other forces.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Can a static magnetic field change a charged particle's kinetic energy?
flashcards.back: No, because q(v cross B) is perpendicular to v and performs no work.
flashcards.reasoning: It changes momentum direction while preserving speed.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is the work-energy theorem?
flashcards.back: Net work on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy.
flashcards.reasoning: It follows by dotting Newton's second law with displacement and integrating.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: When does a force deliver zero instantaneous power?
flashcards.back: When it is perpendicular to the velocity.
flashcards.reasoning: Power is F dot v, so only the parallel component transfers kinetic energy instantaneously.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How does a conservative force point relative to its potential?
flashcards.back: Down the potential gradient: F equals minus grad U.
flashcards.reasoning: A conservative force accelerates the system toward lower potential energy.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How does an effective potential reveal allowed radial motion?
flashcards.back: Motion is allowed where E is at least U_eff; equality marks radial turning points.
flashcards.reasoning: The remaining difference is nonnegative radial kinetic energy.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: When is system momentum approximately conserved during a collision?
flashcards.back: When external impulse is negligible over the short collision interval.
flashcards.reasoning: Internal collision forces exchange momentum but do not change total system momentum.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What extra condition distinguishes an elastic collision?
flashcards.back: Total kinetic energy is conserved in addition to momentum.
flashcards.reasoning: Momentum conservation alone applies to both elastic and inelastic isolated collisions.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What determines center-of-mass acceleration?
flashcards.back: Only the net external force divided by total mass for a closed fixed-mass system.
flashcards.reasoning: Internal forces cancel from the system momentum balance.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Why is F=m a unsafe for a rocket?
flashcards.back: Mass crosses the system boundary and carries momentum, creating a momentum-flux term.
flashcards.reasoning: The constant-mass derivation does not apply to an open variable-mass system.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What two choices must be stated before calculating angular momentum or torque?
flashcards.back: The origin and the reference frame.
flashcards.reasoning: Both quantities can change when the origin moves or is shifted.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: When is angular momentum about a fixed inertial origin conserved?
flashcards.back: When net external torque about that origin is zero.
flashcards.reasoning: The angular-momentum balance is dL/dt equals external torque.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What two kinetic-energy pieces does a rolling rigid body have?
flashcards.back: Center-of-mass translation and rotation about the center of mass.
flashcards.reasoning: Leaving either term out undercounts the motion.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What does the parallel-axis theorem require?
flashcards.back: One known axis must pass through the center of mass, and the new axis must be parallel.
flashcards.reasoning: The added M d squared term refers specifically to the separation of parallel axes.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Why need angular momentum not point along angular velocity?
flashcards.back: Because the inertia tensor can scale different principal-axis components differently.
flashcards.reasoning: L equals I tensor times omega; only principal-axis or spherical rotations guarantee alignment.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How are principal axes found?
flashcards.back: As eigenvectors of the symmetric inertia tensor; eigenvalues are the principal moments.
flashcards.reasoning: The tensor is diagonal in that orthonormal basis.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Which torque-free principal-axis rotation is unstable?
flashcards.back: Rotation about the intermediate principal moment.
flashcards.reasoning: Small perturbations grow for the middle axis but remain bounded for the largest and smallest axes.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How does fast-top precession scale with spin angular momentum?
flashcards.back: Precession rate is roughly torque divided by spin angular momentum.
flashcards.reasoning: A larger angular momentum vector changes direction more slowly under the same torque.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What are the two independent requirements for rigid-body static equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Zero net force and zero net torque.
flashcards.reasoning: One prevents translation; the other prevents angular acceleration.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How do stress and strain differ?
flashcards.back: Stress is force per area; strain is fractional deformation.
flashcards.reasoning: Stress has pressure units, while strain is dimensionless.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is the gravitational field inside a spherical shell?
flashcards.back: Zero everywhere inside.
flashcards.reasoning: Symmetric contributions cancel, though the gravitational potential remains a nonzero constant.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Why do tides scale as inverse distance cubed for a point mass?
flashcards.back: Tides are spatial differences of an inverse-square field, so they involve its derivative.
flashcards.reasoning: Differentiating GM/r squared introduces another factor of 1/r.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is the relation between circular and escape speed at one radius?
flashcards.back: Escape speed is square root of two times circular speed.
flashcards.reasoning: Circular total energy is negative; escape requires raising it to zero.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is the physical meaning of reduced mass?
flashcards.back: It is the effective inertia of the relative separation coordinate in a two-body problem.
flashcards.reasoning: Center-of-mass and relative motion separate, leaving a one-particle central-force equation with mu.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What identifies simple harmonic motion near equilibrium?
flashcards.back: A restoring force linear in displacement, or a potential with positive quadratic curvature.
flashcards.reasoning: The resulting equation is x-double-dot plus omega squared x equals zero.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Where is speed largest in SHM?
flashcards.back: At equilibrium.
flashcards.reasoning: Potential energy is smallest there, so fixed total energy puts the most into kinetic energy.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What are the two pieces of a driven oscillator's motion?
flashcards.back: A decaying transient and a sustained steady-state response.
flashcards.reasoning: They are the homogeneous and particular solutions of the linear differential equation.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What does a large quality factor mean?
flashcards.back: Weak damping, slow energy loss, and a narrow resonance.
flashcards.reasoning: Q is proportional to stored energy divided by energy lost per cycle.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Why is Fourier decomposition useful for a linear oscillator?
flashcards.back: Each harmonic can be solved independently and the responses superposed.
flashcards.reasoning: Linearity lets the system act as a frequency-dependent filter.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What symmetry removes sine coefficients from a Fourier series?
flashcards.back: Even symmetry about the chosen origin.
flashcards.reasoning: An even function times an odd sine integrates to zero over a symmetric period.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How do you read the direction of A cos(kx minus omega t)?
flashcards.back: It travels in the positive x direction.
flashcards.reasoning: Holding phase constant gives x=(omega/k)t plus a constant.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What sets wave speed on an ideal string?
flashcards.back: The square root of tension divided by linear mass density.
flashcards.reasoning: Tension supplies restoring force and linear density supplies inertia.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What boundary condition holds at a fixed string end?
flashcards.back: Transverse displacement is zero, so the end is a node.
flashcards.reasoning: The allowed modes must satisfy the physical endpoint constraint at all times.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Which harmonics occur in an ideal tube closed at one end and open at the other?
flashcards.back: Odd harmonics only.
flashcards.reasoning: A displacement node at one end and antinode at the other fit odd quarter-wavelengths.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: How does isotropic sound intensity scale with distance?
flashcards.back: As one over distance squared.
flashcards.reasoning: The same power spreads across a sphere whose area is 4 pi r squared.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What must a correct Doppler result do for approach?
flashcards.back: Increase the observed frequency.
flashcards.reasoning: Wavefronts arrive more frequently when source and observer approach.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is varied in the calculus of variations?
flashcards.back: An entire admissible function or path, not just a finite parameter.
flashcards.reasoning: Stationarity requires the first-order functional change to vanish for every allowed small variation.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Does stationary action always mean the action is a minimum?
flashcards.back: No. It may be a minimum, maximum, or saddle.
flashcards.reasoning: The Euler-Lagrange equation enforces zero first variation, not the sign of the second variation.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What should be done before writing a Lagrangian?
flashcards.back: Count degrees of freedom and choose independent generalized coordinates.
flashcards.reasoning: Constraints and coordinate dependence determine both kinetic energy and the number of equations.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What are the units of a generalized force conjugate to an angle?
flashcards.back: Torque or energy units.
flashcards.reasoning: Virtual work is Q_theta times delta theta, and angle is dimensionless.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is conserved when a coordinate is absent from L?
flashcards.back: Its conjugate canonical momentum.
flashcards.reasoning: The Euler-Lagrange equation reduces to p-dot equals zero.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: When is the Lagrangian energy function conserved?
flashcards.back: When L has no explicit time dependence, assuming the modeled dynamics are conservative.
flashcards.reasoning: Along motion, dE_L/dt equals minus partial L/partial t.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Which rotating-frame apparent force does no work?
flashcards.back: The Coriolis force.
flashcards.reasoning: It is perpendicular to the velocity measured in the rotating frame.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: When does the Euler apparent force appear?
flashcards.back: When the frame's angular velocity changes with time.
flashcards.reasoning: It is proportional to minus m times Omega-dot cross r.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What must be eliminated when forming H from L?
flashcards.back: The generalized velocities must be written in terms of q, p, and t.
flashcards.reasoning: A Hamiltonian is a phase-space function, not a mixed q-qdot expression.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What does Liouville's theorem conserve?
flashcards.back: Fine-grained volume in canonical phase space.
flashcards.reasoning: Hamiltonian flow has zero divergence in q-p space.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Which frame measures proper time between two timelike events?
flashcards.back: The frame in which both events occur at the same spatial location, so one clock records both.
flashcards.reasoning: Proper time is a worldline quantity for the clock passing through both events.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Which frame measures proper length?
flashcards.back: The object's rest frame.
flashcards.reasoning: A moving observer must record endpoints simultaneously and measures a shorter parallel length.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is the energy-momentum relation for a photon?
flashcards.back: E equals p c.
flashcards.reasoning: Set invariant mass m to zero in E squared equals p squared c squared plus m squared c fourth.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: Why square total four-momentum in a collision problem?
flashcards.back: It produces a Lorentz-invariant equation valid in any convenient frame.
flashcards.reasoning: The invariant mass of the whole system avoids transforming every component separately.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What should you choose before invoking a conservation law?
flashcards.back: The system and the time interval.
flashcards.reasoning: External work, impulse, or torque depends on what crosses the system boundary and over what interval.

flashcards.subject: Classical Mechanics
flashcards.front: What is the best first response to an unfamiliar mechanics problem?
flashcards.back: Sketch, choose coordinates and system, list constraints and symmetries, then select equations.
flashcards.reasoning: Recognition and modeling prevent unrelated formulas from being combined.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What does the divergence theorem convert?
flashcards.back: A volume integral of divergence into outward flux through the closed boundary.
flashcards.reasoning: It is the three-dimensional bookkeeping rule that connects local source strength to net boundary flow.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Why is div(rhat/r^2) not simply zero everywhere?
flashcards.back: It is zero for r > 0 but equals 4 pi delta^3(r) distributionally at the origin.
flashcards.reasoning: Every sphere around the origin has nonzero flux, so the divergence must contain a point source.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Which way does the Coulomb-field separation vector point?
flashcards.back: From the source element to the field point.
flashcards.reasoning: That choice makes a positive source contribute a field pointing away from itself.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: When is direct field integration preferable to Gauss's law?
flashcards.back: When symmetry does not make E constant or zero on a useful closed surface.
flashcards.reasoning: Gauss's law remains true, but it cannot be solved algebraically for the unknown field without symmetry.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Does zero enclosed charge imply zero electric field?
flashcards.back: No. It implies zero net electric flux through the closed surface.
flashcards.reasoning: External charges can create field entering and leaving with cancelling flux.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What is E immediately outside an electrostatic conductor in vacuum?
flashcards.back: E = (sigma/epsilon0) n, normal to the surface.
flashcards.reasoning: The interior field and tangential field vanish, while the normal jump is sigma/epsilon0.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What direction does E point relative to V?
flashcards.back: Toward decreasing potential: E = -grad V.
flashcards.reasoning: A positive test charge loses potential energy as the field does positive work.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Why is there a factor one-half in U = integral rho V / 2?
flashcards.back: It prevents counting each pair interaction twice.
flashcards.reasoning: The potential at each source includes contributions from the other sources, so a direct sum visits every pair in both orders.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What turns a guessed electrostatic potential into a valid solution?
flashcards.back: It satisfies Poisson or Laplace equation in each region and all required boundary/asymptotic conditions.
flashcards.reasoning: The uniqueness theorem then guarantees no different solution has the same data.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Where may image charges be used as if they were sources?
flashcards.back: Only in the physical region where their potential reproduces the conductor boundary conditions.
flashcards.reasoning: The image configuration is a mathematical replacement, not the actual field inside the removed conductor region.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What term dominates a far electric potential when total charge is nonzero?
flashcards.back: The monopole term Q/(4 pi epsilon0 r).
flashcards.reasoning: It falls as 1/r, more slowly than dipole and higher terms.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: When is an electric dipole moment origin independent?
flashcards.back: When the distribution's total charge is zero.
flashcards.reasoning: Shifting the origin changes p by a term proportional to total charge.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What is shared by capacitors in parallel?
flashcards.back: The same voltage difference.
flashcards.reasoning: Each capacitor is connected to the same pair of nodes.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Before analyzing dielectric insertion, what must you state?
flashcards.back: Whether charge or voltage is held fixed, usually by isolation or a connected battery.
flashcards.reasoning: The energy and force conclusions differ between fixed-Q and fixed-V constraints.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: How do bound volume and surface charge follow from P?
flashcards.back: rho_b = -div P and sigma_b = P dot n.
flashcards.reasoning: Divergence detects dipole imbalance inside; the normal component detects dipoles terminated at a surface.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What source appears in div D?
flashcards.back: Free charge density only: div D = rho_free.
flashcards.reasoning: The polarization contribution is packaged into D, but constitutive information is still needed to recover E.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: How are conventional current and electron drift related?
flashcards.back: They point in opposite directions in an ordinary metal.
flashcards.reasoning: J follows q times carrier velocity, and electrons have negative q.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What is the local rate at which fields deliver energy to matter?
flashcards.back: J dot E, power per volume.
flashcards.reasoning: It is positive when the electric field transfers energy to charges, as in ohmic heating.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What circuit quantity cannot jump across an ideal capacitor?
flashcards.back: Capacitor voltage, unless an impulse current is supplied.
flashcards.reasoning: A finite current changes charge continuously, and V_C = Q/C.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: How do you sanity-check an RC transient formula?
flashcards.back: Evaluate it at t = 0 and t approaching infinity.
flashcards.reasoning: Those limits must reproduce the physical initial capacitor voltage and final DC state.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Can a static magnetic field change a point charge's speed?
flashcards.back: No; q v cross B is perpendicular to v and does no work.
flashcards.reasoning: It can change the direction of momentum while leaving kinetic energy unchanged.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What motion results from v having components parallel and perpendicular to uniform B?
flashcards.back: A helix: circular perpendicular motion plus uniform parallel motion.
flashcards.reasoning: Only the perpendicular component experiences magnetic curvature.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: When does Ampere's law directly determine B?
flashcards.back: When symmetry fixes B's direction and magnitude behavior along a useful loop.
flashcards.reasoning: The law alone gives only a circulation, not the local field at every point.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What does div B = 0 mean geometrically?
flashcards.back: Magnetic field lines do not begin or end; net flux through a closed surface is zero.
flashcards.reasoning: Classical electromagnetism contains no magnetic monopole source term.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Why write B = curl A?
flashcards.back: It automatically enforces div B = 0.
flashcards.reasoning: The divergence of any sufficiently smooth curl vanishes identically.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: How does a localized magnetic dipole field fall with distance?
flashcards.back: As 1/r^3 outside the source.
flashcards.reasoning: The magnetic monopole term is absent, so the dipole is the leading localized steady-current field.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: How do bound currents follow from M?
flashcards.back: J_b = curl M and K_b = M cross n.
flashcards.reasoning: Magnetization represents microscopic current loops whose incomplete cancellation appears as macroscopic bound current.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What source appears in curl H in magnetostatics?
flashcards.back: Free current density.
flashcards.reasoning: The magnetization current is absorbed into H = B/mu0 - M.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What does Lenz's law oppose?
flashcards.back: The change in magnetic flux, not necessarily the existing flux itself.
flashcards.reasoning: The minus sign in Faraday's law makes the induced response resist the imposed change.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Why is an induced electric field nonconservative?
flashcards.back: A time-changing B gives curl E = -partial B/partial t, so its closed-loop integral can be nonzero.
flashcards.reasoning: No single-valued electrostatic potential alone can represent that circulating field.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What circuit quantity cannot jump across an ideal inductor?
flashcards.back: Inductor current, unless an impulse voltage is supplied.
flashcards.reasoning: A finite voltage gives a finite dI/dt through V_L = L dI/dt.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What energy exchange occurs in an ideal LC oscillator?
flashcards.back: Energy alternates between capacitor electric energy and inductor magnetic energy.
flashcards.reasoning: With R = 0 the total Q^2/(2C) + LI^2/2 is conserved.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: At series RLC resonance, what happens to reactances?
flashcards.back: omega L and 1/(omega C) cancel, leaving a purely resistive impedance.
flashcards.reasoning: The current amplitude is then maximal for a fixed source amplitude.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Does an ideal inductor consume average AC power?
flashcards.back: No; its voltage and current are 90 degrees out of phase.
flashcards.reasoning: Energy is stored and returned each cycle, making the average of p(t) zero.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: Why is displacement current needed?
flashcards.back: It makes Ampere's law consistent across changing electric flux and preserves charge conservation.
flashcards.reasoning: Without it, different surfaces spanning the same loop around a charging capacitor would disagree.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What continuity equation follows from Maxwell's equations?
flashcards.back: partial rho/partial t + div J = 0.
flashcards.reasoning: Taking the divergence of Ampere-Maxwell and using div curl B = 0 produces local charge conservation.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What direction does the Poynting vector point?
flashcards.back: In the local direction of electromagnetic energy flow, E cross B.
flashcards.reasoning: Its surface flux measures power leaving or entering a control volume.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What correction is needed when using Maxwell stress to find mechanical force?
flashcards.back: Include the time rate of electromagnetic momentum inside the control volume.
flashcards.reasoning: Surface stress is momentum flux; changing stored field momentum also contributes to the balance.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: How are E, B, and propagation direction oriented in a vacuum plane wave?
flashcards.back: They are mutually perpendicular, with E cross B along propagation.
flashcards.reasoning: The source-free Maxwell equations enforce transverse fields and their handedness.

flashcards.subject: Electricity & Magnetism
flashcards.front: What is the amplitude relation in a vacuum plane wave?
